docs.title: Local Sales
docs.text: Contact your local SICK sales representative for product selection, application advice, pricing, and availability. Visit sick.com and select your country or region to find the local sales contact.

docs.title: Support Portal Case
docs.text:
For technical troubleshooting, open a support case at support.sick.com. Describe the issue, your setup, and the steps needed to reproduce it. Include the part number and serial number from the device's type label, together with the firmware version.

If your device provides a diagnostic-file export, create the file through its configuration interface and attach it to the case. Diagnostic information helps SICK investigate the issue; the available export options depend on the device and firmware.

docs.title: Public Discussion
docs.text:
For general integration questions and sharing experience with other users, join the GitHub Discussions space or start a new discussion.

Discussions are public. Do not post credentials, confidential project data, or diagnostic files containing sensitive information; use a Support Portal case for information that should not be shared publicly.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: Compatible with:  LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

docs.title: Connect the Sensor
docs.text:
1. Connect the sensor directly to the computer with Ethernet. The device must be powered, and at least one LED must be green. For the connector layout and pin assignment, see the electrical connection page for LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, or picoScan100.
  2. Give the computer's Ethernet adapter a static address in the sensor subnet. Leave the computer's gateway empty.

Connect the Sensor: device, IP address, and subnet mask.

Device IP address Subnet mask Sensor 192.168.0.1 255.255.255.0 Computer 192.168.0.100 255.255.255.0

The factory sensor address is 192.168.0.1 for LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, and picoScan100. Check the device label or the saved project documentation if the sensor does not respond at that address.

On Windows, open Settings → Network & internet → Ethernet → IP assignment → Edit, select Manual, enable IPv4, and enter the computer's values:

Example Windows configuration for a direct Ethernet connection.

On Windows, also set the network profile of this adapter to Private. A Public profile blocks inbound UDP data and DDS discovery.

docs.title: Open the Web Interface
docs.text:
Open http://<sensor-ip>/ in Chrome, Edge, or Firefox. With factory settings, use http://192.168.0.1/.

SOPASair Home page opened at 192.168.0.1.

If the page does not load, check the subnet settings above or find the sensor on the network.

docs.title: Log In
docs.text: Reading values needs no login. Changing settings requires a login with an enabled user level. On multiScan200 and picoScan100, the factory state has Maintenance and Authorized Client disabled. Log in as Service first, enable only the levels required by the deployment, and change the default passwords during commissioning.

docs.title: Change the IP Address
docs.text:
To use the sensor in your own network, give it an address in that network:

  1. In the web interface, log in and open Configuration → Connection options.
  2. Set Addressing mode to Static, or to DHCP if a DHCP server assigns the address.
  3. Enter the IP address, Subnet mask, and Default gateway. The IP address must be unique in the network.
  4. Click Apply. The browser loses the connection to the sensor.
  5. If the new address is in another subnet, change the computer's Ethernet adapter accordingly. Then open the web interface at the new address and click Save permanently.

Ethernet settings under Configuration → Connection options.

On the multiScan200, restart the device after changing the static IP address so that Native ROS 2 topics are published correctly.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

This glossary explains the terms, abbreviations, and SICK-specific names used in this guide. Where a term has its own page, the entry links to it.

docs.title: A
docs.text: Term Meaning AAS (Asset Administration Shell) Standardized digital twin of a product with its data sheet, operating instructions, certificates, and CAD data. See Asset Administration Shell. Activation type Setting of an evaluation group that defines when the group is evaluated: always, controlled by digital inputs, or controlled by a telegram. See Field Evaluation. Ambient light image Passive, narrow-band image around 905 nm that the multiScan200 captures through its LiDAR receiver. It is not a camera image. AMR (autonomous mobile robot) Mobile robot that navigates without fixed guidance. A typical application for LiDAR sensors. Angle range filter Filter that limits the output to a horizontal and vertical angle range. See Filter Details. API (application programming interface) Interface through which programs access the sensor, for example REST or CoLa. Authorized Client User level for configuring the sensor in daily operation. See User Levels. AutoIP Method in which the sensor assigns itself an IP address when no DHCP server answers. Azimuth Horizontal angle of a beam (theta).

docs.title: B
docs.text: Term Meaning Beam One measurement direction of the sensor. Each beam can return one or more echoes. Blanking Detection mode of field evaluation: the field is infringed when an object at least as large as the minimum object size is inside the field. Smaller objects are ignored ("blanked"). Blooming False points next to highly reflective objects such as retroreflectors. The multiScan200 blooming filter removes them.

docs.title: C
docs.text: Term Meaning Challenge-response authentication Login method of the REST API. The client requests a one-time challenge and answers with a hash that includes the password; the password itself is not transmitted. See REST Interface. Checksum Value calculated over data to detect transmission errors or changes. CoLa B uses an XOR checksum, the Compact format CRC32, and the device reports MD5 checksums of its software and parameters. See Checksums. CloudCompare Open source software for viewing and processing 3D point clouds. See CloudCompare. CoLa (Command Language) SICK telegram protocol for configuration and data requests. CoLa A uses ASCII text on TCP port 2111, CoLa B binary data on TCP port 2112, and CoLa 2 uses TCP port 2122. See CoLa Interface. CoLa1 Collective name for CoLa A and CoLa B. Compact format SICK binary format for measurement data over UDP or TCP, described by Kaitai Struct definitions. See Compact Format. Contamination indication Function that detects dirt on the optics cover and reports warnings or errors. See Contamination Indication. Contour mode Detection mode of field evaluation that compares the scan with a taught-in reference contour. CRC32 32-bit cyclic redundancy check. Protects each Compact and MSGPACK telegram. Cyclone DDS DDS implementation specified as the ROS 2 middleware for native ROS 2.

docs.title: D
docs.text: Term Meaning Data output Application in SOPASair that configures which measurement data the sensor sends and in which format. DDS (Data Distribution Service) Publish-subscribe middleware used by ROS 2. Native ROS 2 runs a DDS participant on the sensor. Device Not Ready Device state that signals that the sensor does not work correctly. Can be output on a digital output (DRDY). Device search Discovery of sensors in the network through UDP broadcasts on port 30718. See Device Discovery. DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) Protocol with which a network server assigns IP addresses automatically. Diagnostic file File with log entries for in-depth analysis by SICK. Created in SOPASair under Diagnostics. Distance-dependent Field evaluation parameter that decides, based on their axial separation, whether two objects are evaluated separately or merged. See Field Evaluation.

docs.title: E
docs.text: Term Meaning Echo Reflection of one laser pulse. One beam can return several echoes, for example from a raindrop and a wall behind it. Echo filter Filter that selects which echoes are output, for example the first, the last, or all echoes. See Filter Details. EEPROM Non-volatile memory of the sensor. Changes are stored permanently only after WriteEeprom (REST) or mEEwriteall (CoLa). Elevation Vertical angle of a beam (phi). Encoder Rotary sensor on a moving axis. The picoScan150 can read an encoder to build 3D point clouds. See 3D With 2D LiDARs. Evaluation One detection field with its parameters. Up to 48 evaluations can be configured. Evaluation group Set of evaluations that is activated and deactivated together.

docs.title: F
docs.text: Term Meaning Field evaluation On-sensor application that checks whether objects are inside a defined field and reports FREE or INFRINGED. See Field Evaluation. Firmware Software that runs on the sensor. See Firmware Update. Fog filter picoScan100 filter that removes fog echoes at close range. Frame One complete scan. A frame is split into segments for output.

docs.title: I
docs.text: Term Meaning IMU (inertial measurement unit) Built-in sensor that measures acceleration, angular velocity, and orientation. Interlaced mode multiScan200 scan configurations 10 to 12, which combine several scans that are shifted against each other to reach a higher resolution. Interval filter Filter that outputs only every n-th scan.

docs.title: K
docs.text: Term Meaning Kaitai Struct Language for describing binary formats. SICK publishes the Compact format as Kaitai Struct definitions (.ksy).

docs.title: L
docs.text: Term Meaning Layer One horizontal scan line at a fixed elevation angle. Multi-layer devices such as multiScan100 and multiScan200 provide several layers; LRS4000 and picoScan100 have one layer. LiDAR (light detection and ranging) Measurement principle that determines distances from the time-of-flight of laser pulses. LMDscandata CoLa telegram with measurement data. See LMDscandata Format.

docs.title: M
docs.text: Term Meaning Maintenance User level for maintenance tasks. See User Levels. Mean filter Filter that averages the distance of each point over several scans, also called moving average filter. On the multiScan200 it is called high precision mode. See Filter Details. Minimum object size Smallest object that infringes a field in blanking mode. MSGPACK (MessagePack) Binary serialization format; used by multiScan100 and picoScan100 for measurement data. See MSGPACK Format. Multi-echo Ability of the sensor to measure several echoes per beam. Multicast Transmission of one data stream to a group of receivers.

docs.title: N
docs.text: Term Meaning Native ROS 2 Function with which the sensor publishes ROS 2 messages itself over DDS, without a host driver. See ROS Integration. NTP (Network Time Protocol) Protocol for synchronizing the sensor clock with a time server. See Time Synchronization.

docs.title: O
docs.text: Term Meaning OpenAPI Machine-readable description of a REST API. SICK publishes an OpenAPI file for each device.

docs.title: P
docs.text: Term Meaning Particle filter Filter that removes isolated points caused by dust, rain, or snow. See Filter Details. pcap File format for recorded network traffic, created for example with Wireshark. See Wireshark. Performance profile See scan configuration. Perpendicular distance measurement picoScan100 application that measures the distance of objects to a reference line. See Perpendicular Distance Measurement. PLC (programmable logic controller) Industrial controller. See PLC Integration. Point cloud Set of 3D points calculated from the measured distances and angles. PointCloud2 ROS message type for point clouds. Product ID Unique identification of a device from its part number and serial number, reachable at pid.sick.com/{P/N}/{S/N}. PSIRT (Product Security Incident Response Team) SICK team that handles reports of security vulnerabilities. PTP (Precision Time Protocol, IEEE 1588) Protocol for precise time synchronization over Ethernet.

docs.title: Q
docs.text: Term Meaning Quaternion Four values (w, x, y, z) that describe an orientation in 3D. The IMU reports its orientation as a quaternion.

docs.title: R
docs.text: Term Meaning Reflector Highly reflective target, such as a retroreflector. The sensor can mark points on reflectors. Region of interest Area to which an evaluation or a filter is limited. For teach-in, the polygon that bounds where the contour is learned. Remission factor Share of the emitted light that an object reflects back, also called remission. Ranges are specified for a given remission factor, for example 10 %. REST (Representational State Transfer) HTTP-based interface of the sensor for reading and writing variables and calling methods. See REST Interface. RMW (ROS middleware) Layer that connects ROS 2 to a DDS implementation. ROS (Robot Operating System) Open source framework for robot software. See ROS Integration. ROS bag Recording of ROS messages in a file (.bag in ROS 1, .db3 or .mcap in ROS 2). See ROS Bag. RSSI (received signal strength indicator) Measure of the strength of an echo.

docs.title: S
docs.text: Term Meaning Scan configuration Predefined combination of aperture angle (field of view), scanning frequency, and angular resolution, identified by a number. Scan range Angle range covered by the sensor, for example 276° for the picoScan100. ScanSegmentAPI SICK Python and C# libraries for receiving segmented scan data. The Python library supports LRS4000, multiScan100, and picoScan100; the C# library supports multiScan100 and picoScan100. Segment Part of a frame that is sent as one telegram so that it can be processed immediately. Service Highest user level. Enabled on delivery. See User Levels. Session token Token that authorizes binary file transfers, for example firmware updates and configuration backups. sick_perception_sdk SICK C++ SDK for configuring LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, and picoScan100 sensors and receiving Compact data. See Programming Tools and Examples. sick_scan_xd SICK driver for ROS 1, ROS 2, and applications without ROS. See ROS Integration. Slot One column of measurements at a horizontal angle step; on the multiScan200, each slot contains all layers. SOPAS ET SICK Engineering Tool for Windows for configuring and visualizing devices. See SOPAS ET. SOPASair Web interface of the sensor, opened in a browser. See SOPASair. STX / ETX Start of text (0x02) and end of text (0x03), the control characters that frame a CoLa A telegram. Swagger UI Interactive viewer for OpenAPI files. System plug Exchangeable connector unit of the sensor that also stores a copy of the parameters.

docs.title: T
docs.text: Term Meaning Teach-in Function that learns the current environment as the reference contour of a field. See Field Evaluation. Telegram One message exchanged with the sensor, for example a CoLa command or a Compact data packet. Telegram type Number in a Compact telegram that identifies its content, for example scan data or IMU data.

docs.title: U
docs.text: Term Meaning Unicast Transmission of a data stream to one receiver. User level Access level that defines which settings a user can change: Maintenance, Authorized Client, or Service. See User Levels.

docs.title: V
docs.text: Term Meaning Virtual Sensor Lab Browser-based simulation of SICK sensors. See Virtual Sensor Lab.

docs.title: W
docs.text: Term Meaning WebSocket Protocol for a persistent connection over which the sensor pushes events. See WebSocket Events. Wireshark Network analysis tool. SICK provides a Wireshark dissector for the Compact format.

docs.title: X
docs.text: Term Meaning XOR checksum Checksum of CoLa B telegrams: the exclusive OR of all payload bytes.

docs.title: LiDAR Basics
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

LiDAR stands for light detection and ranging. A LiDAR sensor sends out laser pulses and evaluates the light that comes back from objects. Every measurement produces a distance and the direction the beam pointed in, so the sensor maps its surroundings without touching anything.

The sensor supplies its own light. It therefore works in daylight, at night, indoors, and in tunnels. This page explains the measuring principle and the terms used throughout this guide. Short definitions are collected in the glossary.

docs.title: Measuring Distance with Light
docs.text:
The sensor measures the time between the emitted pulse and the received pulse.

A pulse leaves the sender, travels to the object, and part of it returns to the receiver. The sensor measures the elapsed time. Light travels at a known speed and covers the distance twice, so the distance is half the time-of-flight multiplied by the speed of light.

The beam follows a straight line, so the sensor reports the shortest distance to the first object in its path. Two pulse time-of-flight implementations are relevant here:

Measuring Distance with Light: process, how it works, and strength.

Process How it works Strength Single-pulse time-of-flight Determines a distance from the travel time of one pulse and its echo. Direct measurement with a short response time. HDDM+ Combines the returns from many pulses to calculate one distance value. Reliable readings on dark objects and in poor visibility.

Both implementations determine distance from the travel time of light. HDDM+ uses the additional measurements to make the result more robust.

docs.title: How Much Light Comes Back
docs.text:
A rough surface scatters the beam, so only a fraction of the light returns to the receiver.

Most surfaces scatter light in many directions, and only a small part of it reaches the receiver. The share of light that an object sends back is its remission factor. It determines how far away that object can still be measured.

How Much Light Comes Back: surface and approximate remission.

Surface Approximate remission Coal 5 % Matte black shoe leather 10 % White drywall 90 % Reflective tape Several 1,000 % Retroreflector Up to 10,000 %

Scanning ranges are therefore always stated together with a remission factor, for example 30 m at 10 % remission. A dark object is detected at a shorter distance than a bright one, and retroreflectors return far more light than a diffuse surface.

The beam needs a clear line of sight. A LiDAR sensor does not see around corners and generally cannot measure through glass or film packaging. Such surfaces create reflections of their own and disturb the measured value.

docs.title: One Beam, Several Echoes
docs.text:
Fog, rain, and the solid object each produce a different return signal.

A laser pulse is not infinitely thin. When the beam hits a raindrop, a dust cloud, or the edge of an object, part of the light is reflected early while the rest travels on to the surface behind. Every reflection that reaches the receiver is an echo, and the sensor can report more than one echo per beam.

Echoes are what make LiDAR usable outdoors, because reflections from rain, snow, dust, and hail can be separated from the real target. The echo filter selects which echoes the sensor outputs, for example the first echo, the last echo, or all of them.

docs.title: One, Two, and Three Dimensions
docs.text:
One, Two, and Three Dimensions: variant, what it measures, and typical sensor.

Variant What it measures Typical sensor 1D Distance along a single fixed beam. Distance sensor aimed at a target or a reflector. 2D Distance and angle within one plane. 2D LiDAR sensor, also called a laser scanner. 3D Distance, horizontal angle, and vertical angle. Multi-layer sensor, or a 2D sensor that is moved.

The horizontal angle of a beam is called the azimuth and the vertical angle the elevation.

docs.title: How a 2D Sensor Scans a Plane
docs.text:
A rotating mirror sweeps the beam of one sender and receiver across a whole plane.

A 2D sensor deflects its beam with a rotating mirror, so a single sender and receiver cover an entire plane. The sensor fires its pulses in step with the mirror rotation. This links three values: the pulse rate of the laser, the rotation speed of the motor, and the angular resolution.

Angular resolution is the angle between two neighboring measured points.

A fine angular resolution places the measured points closer together.

A fine angular resolution puts the measured points close together and covers the scan plane without gaps, so even small objects are detected. A coarse angular resolution produces fewer points per scan. The beam also widens with distance, so the points move further apart the further away the object is. A scan that covers an area without gaps nearby can leave gaps at long range.

One full scan of the plane is called a frame. The sensors in this guide output each frame in segments, and filters can reduce the data before it is sent. See Data Streaming and Filter Details.

docs.title: From Scan Planes to Point Clouds
docs.text:
A multi-layer sensor scans several planes at once, each tilted by a fixed angle.

A 3D sensor adds the vertical angle. Multi-layer sensors contain several sender and receiver modules aimed at different vertical angles, so one rotation produces several scan planes, called layers, at the same time. Distance, azimuth, and elevation together describe every measured point as an XYZ coordinate. A set of such points is a point cloud.

Modern multi-layer sensors extend this principle with more closely spaced scan planes, giving objects a more detailed three-dimensional shape.

Multiple scan planes provide the spatial coverage needed to build a 3D view.

A 2D sensor can also produce 3D data when it is moved, for example on a rotating axis, a linear axis, or a vehicle. The scans carry time stamps, and the known movement supplies the missing third coordinate. See 3D With 2D LiDARs.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Quick fixes for the problems you are most likely to encounter during commissioning and integration. Each row links to the page with the details. Available settings, protocols, and menu paths vary by device family and firmware. Use the relevant device guide and release notes to confirm support.

docs.title: Connection
docs.text:
Connection: symptom and check.

Symptom Check Sensor not reachable / ping fails Computer and sensor in the same subnet; power and Ethernet connected (Getting Started) IP address unknown Device Discovery: SOPAS ET search, or ARP when device search is disabled Lost connection after an IP change Move the computer to the new subnet, or use device search to find the sensor Web UI does not load Open http://<ip>/ in Chrome, Edge, or Firefox; clear the cache; check that the web server is not disabled (Cybersecurity)

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Configuration: symptom and check.

Symptom Check Cannot change settings in the web UI Log in with an enabled user level; without login, the UI is read-only REST response has header.status 4 (Access Denied) The HTTP status is always 200; check header.status. Fetch a new challenge for every POST, check the password and that the user level is enabled, and wait 30 s after five failed logins (REST Interface) REST file transfer returns 403 Send a valid X-Session-Token header (Backup & Restore) Settings lost after power cycle Persist with WriteEeprom or Save permanently (REST Interface) CoLa sFA error response Look up the CoLa error code Web UI shows an error ID Look up the ID in the Error Codes list Need to restore factory settings How to perform a factory reset

docs.title: Measurement Data
docs.text:
Measurement Data: symptom and check.

Symptom Check No UDP data arrives Data output enabled and destination IP/port set to your computer; Windows network profile set to Private; firewall allows the UDP port (Compact Format) Scan view empty Measurement is active and data output is enabled in the device's web interface CRC errors in your parser Compact: CRC32 over the whole frame; MSGPACK: CRC32 over the MSGPACK buffer only (MSGPACK Format) Fewer points than expected Filters and scan range reduce or zero out points No ROS 2 topics visible on a device with Native ROS 2 support Cyclone DDS configured with the host interface IP; matching domain ID (Native ROS 2) WebSocket closes with error 1002 on a device with WebSocket support Negotiate permessage-deflate (WebSocket Events) Reduced range or warnings Check contamination indication and clean the optics cover

docs.title: Get Support
docs.text: Create a diagnostic file in SOPASair (Diagnostics → Overview → Diagnostic file) and send it to SICK with a description of the problem. See Contact.

docs.title: LRS4000
docs.text:
LRS4000 2D LiDAR sensor.

The LRS4000 is a long-range 2D LiDAR sensor for demanding outdoor applications. This developer section covers the LRS4581R. Use the Product ID (PID) to find the exact product variant on sick.com: enter the part number (P/N) and optional serial number (S/N), for example 1134610/25250710. A complete pid.sick.com URL is also accepted.

Product ID pid.sick.com/ Open product

Supported inputs, onboard processing functions, and outputs for the LRS4000.

Input Processing Output CoLa A/B 3D scan recording CoLa A/B telegrams Digital inputs Contamination indication Compact over TCP Encoder Device discovery Contamination status Ethernet Echo filtering Detection history HTTPS Field evaluation Diagnostic recordings NTP Long-range 2D scanning Digital outputs PTP Mean filtering Field-evaluation states REST API Median filtering LMDscandata over TCP SOPASair Motor synchronization Perpendicular-distance values Particle filtering REST JSON responses Perpendicular distance ROS 2 via sick_scan_xd Range filtering

docs.title: CoLa Telegram Listing
docs.text:
This reference lists the CoLa telegrams supported by the LRS4000. Use the command details to build or troubleshoot PLC and other low-level integrations without guessing the telegram structure. For connection setup, framing, and log in, see CoLa Interface.

Entries follow the telegram order in the LRS4000 operating instructions. Detailed entries list request and response structures, examples, variable types, lengths, and CoLa A and CoLa B values where applicable.

Telegram structure: "Command type" "Command"

Telegram part Description Variable Length Additional details Values CoLa A (ASCII) Values CoLa B (Binary) Lists the different parts of the telegram. Describes the corresponding telegram parts. Defines the type of the variable. Defines the length in byte. Gives further information regarding the values in CoLa A/ CoLa B if necessary. Defines the value of the telegram part in CoLa A (ASCII). Defines the value of the telegram part in CoLa B (Binary).

Commands are colored blue, parameters orange for further differentiation.

Protocol Example CoLa A <"Start of text">"Command type value (ASCII)""space""Command value (ASCII)""space""Parameter value (ASCII)""space""Parameter value (ASCII)"<"End of text"> CoLa A Copy example with framing (ASCII) CoLa A Copy example without framing (ASCII) CoLa A Copy example with framing (Hex) CoLa B "Start of text and given length" "Command type value (Binary)""space""Command value (Binary)""space""Parameter value (Binary)""Parameter value (Binary)""Calculated checksum" CoLa B Copy example without framing (Binary)

docs.title: Read for Frequency and Angular Resolution [sRN LMPscancfg]
docs.text:
Read the scanning frequency, angular resolution and aperture angle of the device. Values show the information of the values before any filters are applied. Therefore aperture angle is always showing the maximum, scanning frequency and angular resolution may also be static depending on device family.

docs.title: Poll One Telegram [sRN LMDscandata]
docs.text:
Asking the device for the measurement values of the last valid scan. The device will respond, even if currently no measurement data is created (e.g. due to standby or log in).

Data is transmitted only via LMDscandata when LMDscandata is selected as data output format.

During the boot up phase of the device, there will be no data telegram or answer from the device.

Important: The sRN LMDscandata and sEN LMDscandata telegrams must not be sent via CoLa A. Use CoLa B for these data telegrams; sending them over CoLa A can result in data loss.

Telegram structure: sRN LMDscandata

Telegram part Description Variable Length Additional details Values CoLa A (ASCII) Values CoLa B (Binary) Command type Read String 3 sRN 73 52 4E Command Only one telegram String 11 LMDscandata 4C 4D 44 73 63 61 6E 64 61 74 61

Example: sRN LMDscandata

Protocol Example CoLa A <STX>sRN{SPC}LMDscandata<ETX> CoLa A <STX>sRN LMDscandata<ETX> CoLa A sRN LMDscandata CoLa A 02 73 52 4E 20 4C 4D 44 73 63 61 6E 64 61 74 61 03 CoLa B 02 02 02 02 00 00 00 0F 73 52 4E 20 4C 4D 44 73 63 61 6E 64 61 74 61 05 CoLa B 73 52 4E 20 4C 4D 44 73 63 61 6E 64 61 74 61

Telegram structure: sRA LMDscandata

The response uses the scan-data structure documented for sRA/sSN LMDscandata below. The sEA LMDscandata telegram is the subscription acknowledgement, not the scan-data payload.

docs.title: Send Data Permanently [sEN LMDscandata]
docs.text:
Start or stop continuous transmission of measurement data. Data is transmitted as configured as soon as measurement data is generated by the device. No data is generated when there is an active log in, the laser is shut off (e.g. in Standby mode), the motor is stopped, the data format is Compact, or the device is in certain error modes (e.g. Device not ready).

Data is transmitted only via LMDscandata when LMDscandata is selected as data output format.

During the boot up phase of the device, there will be no data telegram or answer from the device.

docs.title: Set Time Stamp [sMN LSPsetdatetime]
docs.text:
The data format in the telegram is: +2009{SPC}+7{SPC}+22{SPC}+12{SPC}+0{SPC}+0{SPC}+0.The numbers represent year, month, day, hour, minute, second, microsecond.

If plus is used up-front the data it is interpreted as an integer decimal number, without the plus it's the scanner reads the data as hex format.

The answer is always in ASCII format.

Does only work if NTP- respectively PTP-Client is not active.

There is no real time clock inside the device. When the scanner is switched off and after a reboot, the time has to be set again. Therefore, it is recommended to use a NTP or a PTP setting.

Telegram structure: sMN LSPsetdatetime

Telegram part Description Variable Length Additional details Values CoLa A (ASCII) Values CoLa B (Binary) Command type Method String 3 sMN 73 4D 4E Command Set time stamp String 14 LSPsetdatetime 4C 53 50 73 65 74 64 61 74 65 74 69 6D 65 Year Uint_16 2 +1970d … +2099d (07B2h … 0833h) 07 B2 … 08 33 Month Uint_8 1 +1d … +12d(01h … 0Ch) 01 … 0C Day Uint_8 1 +1d … +31d(01h … 1Fh) 00 … 1F Hour Uint_8 1 +0d … +23d(00h … 17h) 00 … 17 Minute Uint_8 1 +0d … +59d(00h … 3Bh) 00 … 3B Second Uint_8 1 +0d … +59d(00h … 3Bh) 00 … 3B Microsecond Uint_32 4 +0d … +999999d(00000000h … 000F423Fh) 00 00 00 00 … 00 0F 42 3F

Example 2: sMN LSPsetdatetime Date: 26.01.2010; Time: 10:35

docs.title: Electrical Connection
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000

The LRS4000 has separate M12 connectors for power, Ethernet, and digital I/O/encoder signals. The tables below reproduce the assignments from LRS4000 operating instructions 8026337/1VNC, pages 34–35.

docs.title: SOPASair Walkthrough
docs.text:
SOPASair is the built-in web interface of the LRS4000. It runs directly on the sensor, so no software installation is needed. Open http://<sensor-ip>/ in a browser on the same network as the sensor. The factory default address is 192.168.0.1.

You can view status and settings without logging in. To change settings, log in with the Authorized Client user level using the user icon in the top bar.

The SOPASair Home dashboard: device status, live scan view, input and output states, and detection history at a glance.

docs.title: Home
docs.text:
The Home page summarizes the sensor's state. It is a good place to start before you change any settings.

Status shows separate indicators for the device, connection, measurement, field evaluation, and data output. Because each state is reported independently, measurement can be running while external data output is switched off.

Device and application status indicators.

Device information lists the model, part number, serial number, firmware version, system time, and the time of the last save. Click Find device to make the sensor LEDs blink, so you can identify the unit on site.

Device identity and installed firmware version.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: The Configuration menu contains the measurement, filter, network, and I/O settings. For the matching REST parameters and value ranges, see the LRS4000 OpenAPI reference.

docs.title: Basic Settings
docs.text:
Configuration > Basic settings defines how the sensor scans. Select a scan configuration to set the scan rate and angular resolution. The page also shows the angular range, interlaced mode, and maximum scanning range, and lets you adjust sensitivity, the status LED, and the measurement state.

Scan configuration and measurement settings. The values shown are an example configuration.

Date and system time shows the device clock and its synchronization source. Apply computer time sets the sensor clock to your computer's time. For network-based time sources, see Time synchronization.

Device clock and time synchronization settings.

Motor synchronization aligns the rotation of several scanners to avoid mutual interference. Select the synchronization source here when you integrate multiple sensors. See Motor synchronization for setup details.

Motor synchronization source.

docs.title: Filter
docs.text:
Configuration > Filter combines the echo, particle, median, and mean filters. The echo filter selects all, first, or last echoes. Expand each of the other filters to set its threshold, width, or averaging parameters. See Filter details for how each filter affects the measurement data.

Echo, particle, median, and mean filters.

docs.title: Contamination Indication
docs.text:
Configuration > Contamination indication monitors the front window for dirt. The sector diagram shows the contamination state per sector, using the color legend below it. You can configure whether a warning or error is output, the sensitivity, the monitored sectors, and the response delay. See Contamination indication for the application background.

Contamination status per sector and evaluation settings.

docs.title: Connection Options
docs.text:
Configuration > Connection options contains the Ethernet settings: addressing mode, IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, MAC address, and link speed.

When you click Apply, the new network settings take effect immediately. The browser loses its connection if the sensor moves to an address that your computer cannot reach, so note the new address before applying the change.

Ethernet addressing and link settings.

docs.title: Inputs and Outputs
docs.text:
Configuration > Inputs and outputs assigns each port as an input or an output. For outputs, select the signal sources, inversion, logic, and restart behavior. The connector diagram next to each port shows the corresponding pin, and the status indicators show the current physical state. Enable Use encoder if an external encoder is connected.

Port assignments with connector pin diagrams.

docs.title: Applications
docs.text: The Applications menu contains measurement-data output and the on-device applications: field evaluation, 3D scan recording, and perpendicular distance measurement.

docs.title: Data Output
docs.text:
Application > Data output selects the output format: Compact, LMDscandata, or Deactivated. The page lists the protocols and ports on which the data is available. See Data streaming for the transport options and parser requirements.

Output format, protocols, and ports.

Output data format selects the optional content of each telegram: device name, time stamp, encoder values, and RSSI. It also sets the output interval and the distance scaling factor.

Optional telegram content, output interval, and scaling factor.

Output range limits the output to a start and stop angle.

Start and stop angle of the output range.

Range filter removes measurement points outside a distance window.

Distance filter.

docs.title: Field Evaluation
docs.text:
Application > Field evaluation monitors fields for objects and switches outputs when a field is infringed. Each group combines fields, evaluations, and outputs, and has its own activation source. Resource requirements shows how much of the sensor's evaluation capacity is in use, and Detection list shows recent detections.

An evaluation group with its field, evaluation, and output.

Teach-in creates a field automatically from the current environment. Set the distances in front of and behind the detected contour and the minimum teach-in time, then start teach-in from the button or a digital input.

Teach-in parameters and start control.

See Field evaluation for a complete commissioning procedure.

docs.title: 3D Scan Recording
docs.text:
Application > 3D scan recording combines 2D scans with the sensor's rotation to build a 3D point cloud. The rotation comes from the internal IMU or an external encoder. Start the recording with the button or an input signal, and download the resulting point cloud when it is complete.

3D scan recording with the internal IMU as rotation source.

docs.title: Perpendicular Distance Measurement
docs.text:
Application > Perpendicular distance measurement reports the shortest and furthest measuring points within a field, relative to a reference plane. Use Add group to define a new measurement, and Result list for distance measurement to view the results.

A perpendicular-distance measurement group.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Diagnostics > Overview combines status, device identity, operating information, the current device status, and the message log. Expand Operating information to see the number of power-on cycles, the operating hours, and the time of the last parameterization.

Power-on count, operating hours, and last parameterization.

The message table lists current and past events with their status number and description. If you need support, use Create diagnostic file to collect the device state in one file and send it to SICK. See Contact.

docs.title: Cybersecurity
docs.text:
Diagnostics > Cybersecurity shows the HTTPS certificate with its fingerprint, serial number, issuer, and expiry date. Use Create certificate to generate a new certificate. The Hash calculator helps you verify file checksums. See HTTPS and certificates for the complete certificate setup.

HTTPS certificate overview.

docs.title: Data Recorder
docs.text:
Diagnostics > Data recorder explains how to install the SICK data recorder on your computer and connect it to the sensor. Use the recorder to capture measurement data for later analysis or support cases.

Installation and connection steps for the data recorder.

docs.title: Detection History
docs.text:
Diagnostics > Detection history records field-evaluation detections. Select the evaluations to include, then start the history. The Statistics section counts the detections per evaluation, and the Detection list shows each event with its time stamp. Use Reset detection history to clear the counters.

Detection counts per evaluation.

docs.title: Motor Synchronization
docs.text:
Motor synchronization coordinates measurement start angles across several LRS4000 sensors. It can increase the effective scan frequency or resolution of a combined system. The sensor shifts its measurement start angle between −180° and +180°; set the phase for each device individually.

LRS4000 supports two synchronization methods.

docs.title: PTP Synchronization
docs.text: Synchronize the LiDAR sensors over Ethernet to a central PTP master. The sensors then share a system time and operate synchronously. The OpenAPI reference exposes the SyncMode and SyncPhase settings and provides the MotorSyncStatus endpoint.

docs.title: Synchronization Through Inputs and Outputs
docs.text:
Use one LRS4000 as the reference device and configure the remaining devices as synchronized devices.

  1. On the reference device, set the motor synchronization source to No source, define its start angle, and configure an output with the index signal as its source.
  2. On each synchronized device, set the motor synchronization source to Line (index signal at IN1) and define its start angle.
  3. Connect each synchronized device's IN1 to the reference device's output that generates the index signal.

Combine measurement data from multiple devices in the customer application.

docs.title: Check Synchronization Status
docs.text: Read the MotorSyncStatus endpoint in the LRS4000 REST API reference. The documented values distinguish between no clock/rotation synchronization, time synchronization only, and synchronized operation.

docs.title: Release Notes
docs.text: This page summarizes LRS4000 firmware changes, fixes, compatibility notes, and known issues. The releases apply to the LRS4581R. Check the device serial number and firmware version before applying release-specific information.

docs.title: General Information
docs.text: The extended-range capability is available for eligible devices. Firmware from version 1.7.0 supports that mode only on devices produced from November 2024 with serial number SN2442xxxx or higher. Earlier devices may be updated, but do not gain the extended-range feature.

docs.title: Update Instructions
docs.text:
Use SOPAS ET or SICK AppManager for firmware updates. Downgrading firmware is not recommended.

Before updating, unpack the firmware package on the computer, connect the sensor by Ethernet on the same subnet, and maintain a stable power supply. Save the parameter file, add the device to the SOPAS ET project, select Download firmware, and install the appropriate .spk package. After the sensor reboots, verify its firmware version and operation. Follow the complete update procedure for the firmware package before updating a production device.

docs.title: Firmware V1.10.0
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4581R

New features: Redesigned web interface, cybersecurity page, HTTPS for web services, distance-data recording, and Perpendicular Distance.

Improvements: SOPAS ET web-server access and encoder settings presentation.

New features.

  • The web interface was redesigned, and a cybersecurity page was added to show open ports and user levels and manage related settings.
  • Web-server and REST configuration can use HTTPS.
  • Distance-data recording is available through the SICK data recorder; download the software from the device web interface.
  • Perpendicular Distance functionality was added.

Improvements.

  • SOPAS ET can enable a disabled web server and now links to the device web interface instead of emulating it.
  • Encoder settings are shown under inputs and outputs; encoder functionality is unchanged.

Bug fixes.

Invalid device IP ranges are rejected, field-evaluation bugs were corrected, and DHCP fallback behavior was corrected to static IP.

Incompatibilities.

  • sWN EtherCoLaAEventsEnable is no longer available. CoLa A event output is generally allowed, but do not use it for LMDscandata because data may be lost.
  • sWN ScanDataEnable has no effect. Use the data-output format setting to disable output.

Known issues.

Device temperature is displayed as 20 °C in the web interface and by sRN OPcurtmpdev. This display and telegram behavior are planned for removal in a later firmware version.

docs.title: Firmware V1.9.1
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4581R; Release date: 2026-04

Improvements: Softer motor startup after power-on.

Bug fixes.

Field-evaluation group activation through inputs now uses the corrected input-to-group assignment. The release also fixes an overload error at startup when multiple configured groups would overload the device if all were active simultaneously.

Known issues.

After reboot, an IP address in the 169.254.x.x range may cause a fatal device error. Return the device to 192.168.0.1 and install current firmware through SOPAS ET as a recovery procedure.

docs.title: Firmware V1.9.0
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4581R

New feature: Adds Sensitivity Mode.

Sensitivity Mode.

The mode can extend range and improve detection of highly reflective targets. Observe the operating conditions in the table below. Using a mode outside its stated ambient-light conditions may reduce detection probability and increase noise.

Firmware V1.9.0: maximum range in standard and extended-range mode (10% remission) and maximum ambient light per sensitivity mode.

Sensitivity mode Maximum range, standard mode (10% remission) Maximum range, extended-range mode (10% remission) Maximum ambient light Normal 55 m 100 m 80 klux Sensitive 65 m 115 m 30 klux Very Sensitive 70 m 120 m 10 klux

Incompatibilities.

The device temperature sensor was removed. OPcurtmpdev no longer works.

docs.title: Firmware V1.8.1
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4581R

Improvement: Adds an adjustable TCP transmit timeout for CoLa connections.

EtherColaTransmitTimeout adjusts the transmit timeout for TCP connections on ports 2111 and 2112. The default remains 15 seconds; the setting can be changed from 250 milliseconds to 15 seconds to speed reconnection after an unexpected disconnect.

Bug fixes.

The release fixes CoLa A/B commands being ignored after reconnecting over an unstable network on TCP ports 2111 and 2112.

Known issues.

The GUI depicts the input/output connector as male A-coded, although the connector should be female A-coded.

docs.title: Firmware V1.8.0
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4581R

New features: Field-evaluation detection history and teach-in, additional GUI languages, and a cybersecurity tab with a hash calculator.

Improvements: Compact timestamps, date/time interface, and maximum region-of-interest range.

New features.

  • The home page shows field-infringement detection history, with links to related field-evaluation pages.
  • Teach-in can capture a static background manually or through an input. The taught background can be used for blanking and contour evaluation.
  • A detection-list shortcut was added to field evaluation.
  • Chinese, Japanese, and French were added as GUI languages.
  • The cybersecurity tab groups security functions. Its hash calculator is required for changing passwords through CoLa A/B or logging in through a SICK software driver.

Improvements and bug fixes.

The release updates evaluation naming and detection-history presentation, transmits Compact start/stop timestamps as Linux system time, updates the date/time GUI, and increases the maximum region-of-interest range from 200 m to 300 m. It fixes LED enablement not resetting when application defaults are loaded and corrects SOPAS ET device import so parameters are exported.

Known issues.

The input/output connector is depicted as male A-coded in the GUI, but should be female A-coded.

docs.title: Firmware V1.7.0
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4581R; extended-range feature only on eligible production units

New features: Extended-range mode, field evaluation, online help, user-level management, and distance measurement between two points.

New features.

  • Extended-range mode increases measurement distance up to 300 m. It is selected through the scan configuration, which also changes the scale factor. Eligibility is limited to devices produced from November 2024 with serial number SN2442xxxx or higher.
  • Field evaluation supports up to 16 user-defined fields, subject to field shape and concurrent application load.
  • Online help provides topic descriptions and guided tours.
  • Other web-interface user levels can be enabled after logging in at Service level; CoLa A/B user levels are unaffected.
  • The scan view can measure the distance between two points.

Improvements and bug fixes.

The distance filter was renamed Scanning range filter, and the ignored scan area is shown in gray. The 3D scan-recording start/stop control and scan view were updated. Diagnostic messages gained filtering options. A fatal error for certain partial scan configurations with first- or last-echo filtering and a Chromium scan-view compatibility issue were fixed.

Incompatibilities.

The default echo-filter value changed from FIRST_ECHO to LAST_ECHO.

Known issues.

During 3D scan recording, an overtime measurement stop may leave the button showing Stop. Pressing it a second time restores the Start state.

docs.title: Firmware V1.6.0
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4581R

New features: Scan merge, Compact streaming over TCP, motor synchronization, and system diagnosis.

New features.

  • Scan merge creates a 3D point cloud using position and orientation from the internal IMU or an external encoder. A rotation offset can compensate for rotation around a pivot; the recording can be started in the GUI or by a digital input. The resulting point cloud can be downloaded through the browser.
  • Compact streaming was added over TCP port 2115. UDP is not supported for this format on this device, and only one streaming format can be enabled at a time.
  • Motor synchronization can use PTP clock synchronization or a wired index signal. Synchronization is disabled by default; the receiver phase can set the rotation offset.
  • System diagnosis can create a reduced diagnosis after an error or an extended file at Service level.

Improvements.

Robustness was improved for applications that move or swivel the device.

Known issues.

Certain combinations of partial scan configurations and first- or last-echo filtering could cause a fatal device error. This was fixed in V1.7.0. A Chrome scan-view issue was also fixed in V1.7.0.

docs.title: Firmware V1.5.0
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4581R

New features: Particle Filter, Distance Filter, updated scan-data viewer, and a prompt to change default passwords.

New features.

  • Particle Filter removes isolated small-object or noise echoes, such as rain or dust, based on distance steps from neighboring beam angles.
  • Distance Filter limits scans to a configured range; out-of-range echoes receive distance and RSSI values of zero.
  • The scan viewer adds 3D and split views.
  • The interface prompts users to change passwords that are still at their defaults.

Incompatibilities.

Customer passwords from firmware earlier than 1.5.0 are reset to defaults because of updated password handling. The Glare Detection Filter was removed and replaced by Particle Filter.

Known issues.

The fatal-error scan configuration and Chrome scan-view issues from V1.6.0 also apply to this release; both are fixed in V1.7.0.

docs.title: Firmware V1.4.0
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4581R

New features: Contamination Indication, PTP, IMU secondary data, and controls for the web server and CoLaScan/AutoIP.

New features.

  • Contamination Indication monitors 12 sectors around 360 degrees. Thresholds, response time, and weather-protection cover can be configured. Monitoring is available by GUI and telegram; evaluation is inactive by default.
  • PTP synchronization can be enabled through the web interface or the TSCRole CoLa parameter.
  • IMU secondary data can be read or sent as events.
  • The web server can be disabled from connection settings. EnableColaScan can disable CoLaScan/AutoIP and prevent opening port 30178.

Improvements.

The access level for loading factory defaults changed to Service. The 2D scan-view update interval was improved, connection options were consolidated, and Expert Mode was removed.

Bug fixes and incompatibilities.

The UDP port protocol dialect changed to CoLa B, and SOPAS ET parameter export was corrected. This release contains an incompatibility affecting CoLa1.

Known issues.

Firmware V1.4.0 has a known fatal-error issue for certain partial scan configurations with first- or last-echo filtering. Firmware V1.7.0 fixes this issue.

For feature availability and parameter details, use the documentation for the device and firmware version.

docs.title: Beginner Projects
docs.text:
These examples outline how to turn a LiDAR use case into an application. Each starts with a goal, a sensor-to-application data path, and practical steps for prototyping and validation. Level 1 projects introduce guided sensor applications, Level 2 adds 3D evaluation or point-cloud tools, and Level 3 introduces a robotics software stack.

Beginner Projects: level, example, and goal.

Level Example Goal 1 Building security Monitor an area (e.g. a room floor) very precisely. 1 Bulk scan Measure woodchip profiles and calculate volume throughput using belt speed. 2 Reversing Assistant Detect the closest obstacle behind a vehicle and flash the warning LEDs faster as it gets closer. 2 3D Height Measurement Measure body height with a multiScan100 using perpendicular distance above a floor reference. 2 House in 3D Record picoScan 3D point clouds around a house and inspect the exported PCD files. 3 ROS 2 SLAM Build a map and localize a vehicle within it using ROS 2 and SLAM Toolbox.

docs.title: Building Security Example
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 picoScan100

Security access gates form a transition between secure and non-secure areas of an airport. An object-detection check can help identify items left in the gate area before access is granted.

Example security-door installation. The red overlay illustrates the detection area; the inset shows the LiDAR sensor mounting position.

A compact 2D LiDAR sensor can monitor a configured detection zone and report objects that interrupt the scan or differ from a taught reference contour. This can support a security workflow concerned with prohibited items, such as weapons, but LiDAR object detection alone does not identify an object's type or determine whether it is prohibited. Validate detection coverage and performance for the installation and combine it with the required security checks.

docs.title: Suggested Data Path
docs.text: Configure detection zones on the sensor using field evaluation. Use teach-in to capture the surrounding geometry as a reference contour for detection. Keep the scene stable during capture, then validate the evaluation with representative objects and movement.

docs.title: Bulk Scan
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 picoScan100

LiDAR can measure the profile of woodchips or other bulk raw materials on conveyor belts. Mounted above the belt, the sensor continuously scans the material surface. The application determines material height relative to the empty belt.

Example woodchip conveyor installation. The highlighted scan area covers the material profile across the belt.

docs.title: 3D Height Measurement
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100

A multiScan100 can measure the body height of a person in a defined area. The sensor scans the area in 3D, while perpendicular-distance evaluation measures the detected points relative to the floor. The maximum distance inside the evaluation field represents the person's height.

A 3D LiDAR measures people as they pass through a defined detection area.

docs.title: Suggested Data Path
docs.text:
1. Mount the multiScan100 so its field of view covers the measuring area and the top of the person's head remains within the scan range.
  2. Create an evaluation group in Application > Perpendicular distance measurement and draw a field around the measuring area.
  3. Use the floor as the reference plane. Keep walls, door frames, and other fixed objects outside the field so they cannot become the maximum value.
  4. Configure the object-detection settings for stable measurements.
  5. Read the minimum and maximum perpendicular distances from the evaluation result. Use the maximum distance as the measured body height.

For configuration and result-access details, see Perpendicular Distance Measurement.

docs.title: Example Solution
docs.text:
The following screenshot shows the evaluation in SOPASair. The 3D field covers the person above the floor, and the result list reports the minimum and maximum distances for the evaluation.

Height-measurement example using perpendicular distance. The maximum distance of 1766 mm represents the measured body height.

Validate the setup with people of known height and verify that the reported maximum remains stable as a person moves through the measuring area.

docs.title: House in 3D
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 picoScan100

This example shows how to use a picoScan150 3D scan recording as a starting point for documenting a building. The sensor combines its 2D scan profiles with rotation information from its internal IMU or an external encoder and exports the result as a .pcd point-cloud file.

docs.title: Suggested Data Path
docs.text:
The on-device scan merger records one point cloud at a time.

Mount and orient the sensor so its scan plane sweeps the area of interest as it rotates. Configure an IMU or encoder rotation source and the sensor offset in Application → 3D scan recording. Clear the previous recording, capture the sweep, stop recording, and wait for saving to finish. Download /cloud.pcd before starting the next capture; the device keeps only the most recent point cloud.

docs.title: Reversing Assistant
docs.text:
Compatible with: picoScan100

When reversing a vehicle, objects behind it can be difficult to see and the available stopping distance decreases quickly. A LiDAR sensor can monitor this area and provide an immediate warning: the closer the nearest obstacle is, the faster the sensor LEDs flash.

The LiDAR monitors the reversing area. A shorter distance to the nearest obstacle produces a faster warning flash.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
• Connect the picoScan150 and the development computer to the same network.
  • Mount the sensor so its field of view covers the monitored reversing area.
  • Build and install sick_perception_sdk with the picoScan100 examples.
  • Change receiverAddress if the computer does not use 192.168.0.100.
  • This minimal example uses the default Service password servicelevel.

docs.title: Minimal Example
docs.text:
This example is based on the SDK's UDP streaming example. The point-cloud callback only calculates the flash period; the main loop performs the REST writes so scan reception is not blocked by an HTTP request.

The warning uses the radial range supplied by the scanner in the Compact scan data. Every point in the received frame is considered.

Expand to view the complete C++ example 
#include <sick_perception_sdk/compact_format/PointCloud/UnorganizedPointCloud.hpp>
#include <sick_perception_sdk/drivers/picoScan100/PicoScan100Driver.hpp>
#include <sick_perception_sdk/sensor_configuration/HttpClient/httplib_client/HttpClient.hpp>
#include <sick_perception_sdk/sensor_configuration/picoScan150/PicoScan150Configurator.hpp>

#include <atomic>
#include <algorithm>
#include <chrono>
#include <csignal>
#include <cstdint>
#include <limits>
#include <memory>
#include <thread>

// The signal handler changes this flag when the user presses Ctrl+C.
std::atomic<bool> running {true};

int main()
{
  // Change these addresses if the sensor or computer uses another subnet.
  constexpr char sensorAddress[] = "192.168.0.1";
  sick::IpV4Address receiverAddress {"192.168.0.100"};
  constexpr std::uint16_t scanPort = 2115;

  auto const httpClient =
    std::make_shared<sick::httplib_client::HttpClient>(sensorAddress, 80);
  sick::picoScan150::v2_3_3::Configurator configurator(
    httpClient, sick::UserLevel::Service, "servicelevel");

  configurator.enableScanDataStreamingCompactUdp(receiverAddress, scanPort);

  // The scan callback writes these values while the main loop reads them.
  std::atomic<int> flashPeriodMs {0};
  std::atomic<std::chrono::steady_clock::time_point> lastFrame {
    std::chrono::steady_clock::time_point {}};

  // Request the scanner-provided radial range for every point.
  sick::point_cloud::PointCloudConfiguration pointCloudConfig;
  pointCloudConfig.fields.enableSpherical = true;

  sick::picoScan100::Driver driver;
  driver.scanDataReceiver()
    .setup(scanPort)
    .setOnNewFrameCallback(
      [&](sick::point_cloud::UnorganizedPointCloud const& cloud) {
        // Find the closest valid radial range in the complete scan frame.
        float nearest = std::numeric_limits<float>::infinity();
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < cloud.numberOfPoints(); ++i)
        {
          nearest = std::min(nearest, cloud.getRange(i));
        }

        // Store one full LED on/off period for the selected warning level.
        flashPeriodMs =
          nearest <= 0.5F ? 333 :
          nearest <= 2.0F ? 500 :
          nearest < std::numeric_limits<float>::infinity() ? 2000 : 0;
        lastFrame = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
      },
      pointCloudConfig);
  driver.run();

  std::signal(SIGINT, [](int) { running = false; });
  bool ledOn = false;
  while (running)
  {
    // Treat missing scan data as "no obstacle" after 500 ms.
    bool const scanIsCurrent =
      std::chrono::steady_clock::now() - lastFrame.load() <=
      std::chrono::milliseconds(500);
    int const period = scanIsCurrent ? flashPeriodMs.load() : 0;

    if (period == 0)
    {
      if (ledOn)
      {
        configurator.setLEDEnable(false);
        ledOn = false;
      }
      std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(50));
      continue;
    }

    // Toggling after half a period produces the requested flash frequency.
    ledOn = !ledOn;
    configurator.setLEDEnable(ledOn);
    std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(period / 2));
  }

  configurator.setLEDEnable(true);
}

Add the source as another picoScan100 example target and link it with sick_perception_sdk::drivers and sick_perception_sdk::sensor_configuration, like the SDK's data_streaming_udp example. Stop it with Ctrl+C; the final call enables the LEDs again, which is their default state.

docs.title: Expected Behavior
docs.text:
If no scan frame arrives for 500 ms, the scan is treated as stale and the LEDs are switched off.

Expected Behavior: nearest point, flash frequency, and result.

Nearest point Flash frequency Result No obstacle or stale scan Off LEDs stay off 0 m to 0.5 m 3 Hz Fast warning More than 0.5 m to 2 m 2 Hz Medium warning More than 2 m 0.5 Hz Slow warning

Move a test object through the sensor's field of view and check that the reported behavior changes monotonically: every smaller distance must produce the same or a shorter period. Test only in a controlled area; this example is a warning aid, not a safety function.

docs.title: Optional Digital Output
docs.text: The same ledOn value can be sent to POST /api/SetOutput at the same cadence. First configure that output's source as SOPAS command, then call the SDK's setOutput() method with the output number and value. Do not use OutputState for this: that endpoint only reads the current output states.

docs.title: Localization with ROS 2 and SLAM Toolbox
docs.text:
Compatible with: picoScan100

Reliable localization is essential for autonomous driving, driverless-vehicle navigation, and a smooth material flow. High-resolution LiDAR measurements help map the surroundings. Localization software compares measurements with the map to estimate the vehicle's position and orientation, also called its pose. Accuracy depends on the environment, sensor setup, and software configuration.

Illustration of LiDAR mapping and localization with a mobile robot, occupancy map, and pose estimate.

docs.title: ROS 2 for Beginners
docs.text:
For the simplest setup, run this example on an Ubuntu system supported by your ROS 2 distribution. ROS 2, SLAM Toolbox, and RViz are readily available as packages on supported Ubuntu releases. Match the Ubuntu version to the ROS 2 distribution's installation requirements.

ROS 2 is a software framework for connecting robot components. It is not a complete robot application: you combine programs called nodes to handle tasks such as receiving sensor data, estimating position, and driving motors. Nodes exchange messages over named topics.

For this example, a LiDAR integration publishes scan measurements. Mapping or localization software consumes those measurements together with robot motion information. Coordinate transforms (TF) describe how the sensor, robot, and map are positioned relative to one another.

docs.title: Mapping, Localization, and Navigation
docs.text:
Mapping, Localization, and Navigation: task and what it does.

Task What it does SLAM Simultaneous localization and mapping: builds a map while estimating the robot's pose. Localization Estimates the robot's pose within an existing map. Navigation Uses the pose and a destination to plan and follow a route while considering obstacles.

This example only builds a map and estimates the vehicle's pose within it. Use SLAM Toolbox for both stages: first run mapping, then load the saved pose graph in localization mode. A navigation stack, route planner, and motion controller are not required for this example.

docs.title: Suggested Data Path
docs.text:
The typical data path is:

LiDAR LaserScan → scan-matching odometry + TF → SLAM Toolbox → map-relative pose in RViz

This example uses LiDAR scan matching to estimate movement, without wheel encoders. Run a separate scan-matching odometry node alongside SLAM Toolbox; excluding encoders does not remove SLAM Toolbox's odometry requirement. Provide a suitable LaserScan topic to both nodes.

docs.text:
