How to receive IMU data and dissect it with Wireshark.

  • How to use Wireshark to dissect Compact data

docs.title: Filter Details
docs.text:
Filters run on the sensor and change the measurement data before it is sent. Use them to reduce bandwidth, remove unwanted points, and keep the data your application needs. The available filters and their settings differ between devices; each section lists the devices it applies to.

Filter Details: filter, effect, side effect, and devices.

Filter Effect Side effect Devices Interval Sends only every n-th scan Lower output rate multiScan100, multiScan200, picoScan150 Fog Removes fog echoes at close range - multiScan100, picoScan150 Echo Selects which echoes are sent - LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, picoScan150 Particle Removes dust, rain, and snow hits Device-specific settings and latency LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, picoScan100 Moving average Averages distances over several scans Delayed output multiScan100, multiScan200, picoScan150 Blooming Removes blooming artifacts next to highly reflective objects - multiScan200 Angle range Keeps beams inside a horizontal and vertical angle range - multiScan100, multiScan200, picoScan150 Layer Removes complete scan layers from the output Reduced vertical coverage multiScan100 Vertical FoV Keeps nested vertical regions at different resolutions Raw stream only multiScan200 Angle range focus Keeps a 3D angle range with an optional full-resolution region Raw stream only multiScan200 Rectangular Keeps points inside an X/Y rectangle Other points set to 0; data size unchanged multiScan100, picoScan150 Distance Keeps points inside a radial range Other points set to 0; data size unchanged LRS4000, multiScan100, picoScan150 Ground Filters ground returns with configurable thresholds Variant and configuration dependent multiScan100 Mean Averages measurement data Device-specific behavior LRS4000 Median Applies a median filter to measurement data Device-specific behavior LRS4000

The filters run one after another, each on the result of the previous one. For exact parameter names and value ranges, see the product's OpenAPI reference: LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, or picoScan100.

docs.title: Interval Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

The interval filter reduces the scan output rate by a configurable reduction factor from 2 to 50. For example, a factor of three outputs only every third scan, reducing the output rate to one third. On picoScan100, this REST setting is exposed by the picoScan150 OpenAPI.

docs.title: Fog Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100 picoScan100

The fog filter removes unwanted echoes at close range (approximately 3 m). This reduces false activations in fog. On picoScan100, this REST setting is exposed by the picoScan150 OpenAPI. The multiScan200 has no configurable fog filter.

docs.title: Echo Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

The echo filter suppresses measurement data caused by edge hits, rain, dust, snow, and other ambient conditions. Pulses attributed to undesirable ambient conditions are not output. The selectable echoes differ by device:

Echo Filter: device and selectable echoes.

Device Selectable echoes picoScan150 First echo, last echo, or all echoes multiScan200 First echo, last echo, strongest echo, all echoes, or all echoes with the strongest first LRS4000, multiScan100 Read the selectable echo options for the installed firmware in the device's OpenAPI description.

On the multiScan200, field evaluation always uses a single echo. If all echoes are selected, field evaluation uses the first echo.

Example of retaining or suppressing an echo caused by ambient conditions.

docs.title: Particle Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

The particle filter suppresses small, irrelevant reflection pulses caused by dust, raindrops, snowflakes, and similar particles. The filter settings differ by device.

Particle Filter: device and settings.

Device Settings LRS4000 On/off and a distance-step threshold from 500 to 5000 mm multiScan100 On/off and a distance-step threshold from 20 to 5000 mm multiScan200 On/off, a distance threshold from 20 to 2000 mm, and the minimum number of neighbors from 0 to 8 picoScan100 On/off and a distance-step threshold from 20 to 5000 mm

For LRS4000, multiScan100, and picoScan100, the threshold is the required distance step between the echo to be filtered and the echoes of surrounding beam angles. On multiScan200, a point needs at least the configured number of neighboring measurements within the distance threshold. In interlaced multiScan200 scan configurations (10 to 12), the filter compares measurements from different angular positions, so its effect can change. In the Compact format (telegram type 6), bit 6 of the multiScan200 echo properties marks points detected as particles.

docs.title: Moving Average Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

On picoScan150, the moving average filter smooths distance values by calculating the arithmetic mean over several scans of the same point. Configure an averaging depth of two to four scans. The first value is output only after the configured number of scans; invalid distance values (0) are excluded from the average.

Example of a four-scan moving average for representative angular positions (distance values in mm):

Moving Average Filter: scan/output, angle 3, angle 4, angle 5, angle 6, angle 7, and angle 8.

Scan/output Angle 3 Angle 4 Angle 5 Angle 6 Angle 7 Angle 8 Scan 1 1100 1100 1150 1150 1380 1380 Scan 2 1200 1200 1190 950 1500 1500 Scan 3 1150 1450 1200 1200 1450 1450 Scan 4 1170 1170 1220 1220 1470 1150 1. Output (scans 1–4) 1155 1230 1190 1130 1450 1370 Scan 5 0 1110 1150 1150 1380 1380 2. Output (scans 2–5) 1173 1233 1190 1130 1450 1370 Scan 6 1200 1210 1190 0 1500 1500 3. Output (scans 3–6) 1173 1235 1190 1190 1450 1370 Scan 7 1150 0 1200 1200 1450 1450 4. Output (scans 4–7) 1173 1163 1190 1190 1450 1370

Individual outliers still influence the average. Invalid distance values (0) are excluded, so fewer scans contribute at those positions (for example angle 3 in the 2nd output: (1200 + 1150 + 1170) / 3 = 1173).

On multiScan200, the moving average filter is called high precision mode and can only be switched on or off. It averages the distance of each point over several scans, which reduces distance noise while the output rate stays the same. The output is delayed by about 0.5 s. If the distance of an object changes significantly, averaging stops for that object. Use it for static scenes only. It has no effect in interlaced scan configurations (10 to 12).

On multiScan100, the REST API exposes LFPmovingAveragingFilter. Check the OpenAPI description for the available averaging depth and limits for the installed firmware.

docs.title: Blooming Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan200

Highly reflective objects such as retroreflectors can create false points next to the object (blooming). The blooming filter removes them. Select the strength low, medium (default), or strong. In the Compact format (telegram type 6), bit 2 of the echo properties marks points detected as blooming.

docs.title: Angle Range Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

The angle range filter limits the output to a horizontal (theta) and vertical (phi) angle range. A beam increment outputs only every n-th beam.

Angle Range Filter: comparison criterion, multiScan100, multiScan200, and picoScan150.

multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan150 Horizontal range See OpenAPI −180° to +180° −138° to +138° Vertical range See OpenAPI −90° to +90° −90° to +90° Beam increment See OpenAPI 1 to 50, separately for horizontal and vertical 1 or more

On multiScan200, beams outside the range are not transmitted, which reduces the data size. The ambient-light image is limited in the same way.

docs.title: Layer Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100

The multiScan100 layer filter removes complete scan layers from the output data. Configure one Boolean value per layer through LFPlayerFilter; only enabled layers are serialized. This reduces the data volume when an application needs only part of the sensor's vertical coverage. The filter changes the output, not the physical scan performed by the sensor.

docs.title: Vertical FoV Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan200

The multiScan200 CoLa command verticalAngleRangeFilter restricts raw streaming data to an outer vertical region of interest (ROI). An optional inner ROI must lie completely inside the outer ROI. Each region has its own layer increment from 1 to 50, so the inner region can retain more vertical detail while the surrounding region is subsampled more strongly. Layers outside the outer ROI are not transmitted.

The filter also limits ambient-light data. In Full mode, the remaining ambient-light region keeps its full vertical resolution. In Matching mode, its vertical resolution matches the primary measurement data, with one ambient-light pixel per beam.

docs.title: Angle Range Focus Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan200

The multiScan200 angleRangeFocusFilter restricts raw streaming data to a 3D field of view defined by horizontal (theta) and vertical (phi) limits. Beams outside this range are not transmitted. Separate horizontal and vertical increments from 1 to 50 can subsample the remaining data.

An optional focus region preserves full resolution inside a smaller horizontal or vertical region while the surrounding data remains subsampled. This filter affects raw data streaming only and does not affect field evaluation.

docs.title: Rectangular Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100 picoScan100

After the measurement filters, data-reduction settings and the region of interest filter limit the points passed on for further processing. On picoScan100, this REST setting is exposed by the picoScan150 OpenAPI.

When the rectangular filter is active, only scan parts within the rectangle are retained. The filter does not reduce the data; points outside the rectangle are set to zero. Adjust the rectangle by setting the minimum and maximum X and Y values in millimeters.

docs.title: Distance Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 picoScan100

The distance filter limits the measured radial distance and therefore affects a circular area around the product. It does not reduce the data; points outside the selected radial range are set to zero. To keep a circular area, set the maximum range to the required radius in millimeters. To keep a ring, set the maximum range to the required radius and the minimum range to a value greater than 0 mm. On picoScan100, this REST setting is exposed by the picoScan150 OpenAPI.

docs.title: Ground Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100

The multiScan100 REST API exposes groundFilterEnable, groundFilterThresholds, and groundFilterType. The filter can reduce false field-evaluation triggers caused by the ground while retaining detection of small objects when configured correctly. The ground filter is not applied to the raw measurement-data streaming path. Availability can depend on the variant and software package. See multiScan100 release notes and the multiScan100 OpenAPI reference.

docs.title: Mean Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000

The LRS4000 firmware 1.10.0 OpenAPI description exposes a MeanFilter setting. Use that reference for its parameters and permitted values.

docs.title: Median Filter
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000

The LRS4000 firmware 1.10.0 OpenAPI description exposes an LFPmedianfilter setting. Use that reference for its parameters and permitted values.

docs.title: LMDscandata Format
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 picoScan100

LMDscandata is a scan data telegram of SICK's CoLa interface. LRS4000 and picoScan100 expose it as a selectable scan data format. On picoScan100 it is sent over a TCP connection that the client opens to the sensor, so delivery is ordered and error-checked. Use it for PLCs and integrations that already use CoLa. For new high-rate integrations, use Compact or MSGPACK over the transport supported by the device.

docs.title: Receive LMDscandata
docs.text:
1. Select LMDscandata as the measurement data output format (sWN ScanDataFormat, or in SOPASair under Application > Data output).
  2. Open a TCP connection to the sensor: port 2111 for CoLa A or 2112 for CoLa B.
  3. Request data:

Receive LMDscandata: telegram and result.

Telegram Result sRN LMDscandata Returns one scan (polling) sEN LMDscandata 1 Starts continuous output: one telegram per scan sEN LMDscandata 0 Stops continuous output

No data is sent during boot-up or in some error states (for example Device Not Ready). A login session does not block the output. RSSI in LMDscandata is 8-bit; the value 254 marks a detected reflector.

If the output format is not set to LMDscandata, sRN LMDscandata still returns an sRA LMDscandata telegram, but every field is 0. There is no error code, so check the output format first when you only receive zeros.

docs.title: Angle Reference
docs.text: LMDscandata uses the CoLa angle convention: 90° points straight ahead along the sensor X axis. Compact, MSGPACK, and the REST API use 0° for straight ahead. The same full scan of the picoScan100 therefore starts at -48° in LMDscandata and at -138° in Compact. Subtract 90° from an LMDscandata angle to compare it with Compact or MSGPACK data. The start angle and the angular step in the telegram are given in 1/10000°.

docs.title: Configure and Parse
docs.text:
• Configure the picoScan100 telegram content, such as the echoes and RSSI, with sWN LMDscandatacfg. Smaller telegrams reduce PLC load.
  • The picoScan100 field layout is in the picoScan100 CoLa Telegram Listing.
  • For TCP stream parsing (partial and concatenated telegrams), follow PLC Integration.

docs.title: MSGPACK Format
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100 picoScan100

MSGPACK encodes the measurement data with the MessagePack standard. Unlike Compact, it is self-describing: every field has a keyword, so any standard MessagePack library can parse it without knowing the exact layout. The price is more bandwidth than Compact.

Like Compact, each data package carries one scan segment. Each segment can be processed on its own for low latency; collect all segments with the same FrameNumber to get a complete scan. See multiScan100 segments and picoScan100 segments for device-specific behavior.

SICK's Python ScanSegmentAPI (scansegmentapi/msgpack.py) is the reference implementation of this format.

docs.title: Framing
docs.text:
Each MSGPACK buffer is wrapped in a frame. Size and checksum are little-endian uint32 values.

Framing: offset, size, and content.

Offset Size Content 0 4 bytes 02 02 02 02 (4 × <STX>) 4 4 bytes Size n of the MSGPACK buffer in bytes (without the checksum) 8 n bytes MSGPACK buffer 8 + n 4 bytes CRC32 over the MSGPACK buffer only, without the STX bytes and the size

docs.title: MSGPACK Keywords
docs.text:
To save bandwidth, keywords are encoded as uint8 codes instead of strings. Map the codes back to names with the table below. After removing the framing, parse the buffer with a standard MessagePack parser. Some parsers must be told to accept integer map keys; in Python:

unpacked = msgpack.unpackb(msgpack_buffer, strict_map_key=False)

docs.title: Used MSGPACK Keywords and Associated uint8 Codes
docs.text:
Names follow the SICK reference implementation. Some examples use different capitalization, such as TimeStampStart or PropertyValues; on the wire only the code is sent.

Used MSGPACK Keywords and Associated uint8 Codes: keyword name, code, and description.

Keyword name Code Description class 0x10 Class name of the map: Scan or ScanSegment (ScanSegment, Scan) data 0x11 Data part of a ScanSegment, Scan, or array (arrays) numOfElems 0x12 Number of elements in an array elemSz 0x13 Size of one array element in bytes endian 0x14 Endianness of the array elements elemTypes 0x15 Type of the array elements little 0x30 Value: little-endian float32 0x31 Value: data type float32 uint32 0x32 Value: data type uint32 uint8 0x33 Value: data type uint8 uint16 0x34 Value: data type uint16 int16 0x35 Value: data type int16 ChannelTheta 0x50 Channel with azimuth angles ChannelPhi 0x51 Channel with elevation angles DistValues 0x52 Channel with distance values RssiValues 0x53 Channel with RSSI values PropertiesValues 0x54 Channel with beam properties, for example reflector Scan 0x70 Class name Scan TimestampStart 0x71 Time stamp of the first beam of a scan TimestampStop 0x72 Time stamp of the last beam of a scan ThetaStart 0x73 Azimuth angle of the first beam of a scan ThetaStop 0x74 Azimuth angle of the last beam of a scan ScanNumber 0x75 Scan number ModuleID 0x76 ID of the measuring module BeamCount 0x77 Number of beams in a scan EchoCount 0x78 Number of echoes in a scan ScanSegment 0x90 Class name ScanSegment SegmentCounter 0x91 Segment number FrameNumber 0x92 Frame number Availability 0x93 Availability of a segment SenderId 0x94 Sender ID (device serial number) SegmentSize 0x95 Segment size SegmentData 0x96 Array with the measurement data per layer LayerId 0xA0 Array with layer IDs TelegramCounter 0xB0 Telegram counter TimestampTransmit 0xB1 Transmit time stamp

docs.title: Serialization of a Segment
docs.text:
Each data package carries one ScanSegment. Its SegmentData array holds one Scan per layer of the sensor:

ScanSegment
├── TelegramCounter
├── TimestampTransmit
├── SegmentCounter
├── FrameNumber
├── Availability
├── SenderId
├── LayerId
└── SegmentData
    ├── Scan 1
    ├── Scan 2
    ├── ...
    └── Scan N

Metadata fields are plain MessagePack values. Measurement arrays (distances, RSSI, angles, properties) are an exception: they are stored as binary blobs, see Serialization Of Arrays.

docs.title: Notation Used
docs.text:
The following notes on the notation used relate to the description of the structures encoded in MSGPACK:

  • msgpack_map_header denotes the header of a MessagePack map, see the MessagePack specification.
  • Names correspond to the keyword table; on the wire, each name is its uint8 code.
  • Angle brackets mark placeholders, for example <numOfElems> for the number of array elements.
  • The structures are written in a JSON-like notation, but the data is encoded according to the MessagePack specification.

docs.title: Serialization of the ScanSegment Class
docs.text:
The ScanSegment class is represented as a nesting of MSGPACK maps as follows:

msgpack_map_header {
  "class": ScanSegment,
  "data": msgpack_map_header {
    "TelegramCounter": <telegramCounter>,
    "TimestampTransmit": <timestampTransmit>,
    "SegmentCounter": <segmentCounter>,
    "FrameNumber": <frameNumber>,
    "Availability": <availability>,
    "SenderId": <senderId>,
    "LayerId": <layerIdVector>,
    "SegmentData": <segmentData>
  }
}

The meaning of the individual fields is shown in the following table.

Serialization of the ScanSegment Class: name, type, and description.

Name Type Description TelegramCounter MSGPACK int Counts all telegrams with measurement data sent in MSGPACK format since switching on the device. The counter starts at 1. TimestampTransmit MSGPACK int Sensor system time in µs since 1.1.1970 00:00 in UTC. SegmentCounter MSGPACK int Index of the segment within the frame. FrameNumber MSGPACK int Counts the number of full revolutions since the device was started. Availability MSGPACK int Reserved SenderId MSGPACK int Device serial number. It can be used to detect on the recipient which sensor the data was sent from. LayerId MSGPACK array of int Array of layer indices. The layer indices start at 1 and increase with decreasing elevation angle. SegmentData MSGPACK array of scans Array of elements of the Scan class (see Serialization Of The Scan Class) that contain the actual measurement data. The following applies: The scan at position i has the layer number LayerId[i].

The arrays LayerId and SegmentData are MSGPACK arrays as per the MSGPACK specification and are not represented like arrays containing measurement data (see "Serialization of arrays").

docs.title: Serialization of the Scan Class
docs.text:
The Scan class is represented as a nesting of MSGPACK maps as follows:

msgpack_map_header {
  "class": Scan,
  "data": msgpack_map_header {
    "TimestampStart": <timestampStart>,
    "TimestampStop": <timestampStop>,
    "ThetaStart": <thetaStart>,
    "ThetaStop": <thetaStop>,
    "ScanNumber": <scanNumber>,
    "ModuleID": <moduleId>,
    "ChannelTheta": <channelTheta>,
    "ChannelPhi": <channelPhi>,
    "DistValues": <distValues>,
    "RssiValues": <rssiValues>,
    "PropertiesValues": <propertiesValues>,
    "BeamCount": <beamCount>,
    "EchoCount": <echoCount>
  }
}

The meaning of the individual fields is shown in the following table:

Serialization of the Scan Class: name, type, and description.

Name Type Description TimestampStart MSGPACK int Acquisition time of the first beam of the scan in µs. The device's internal time base is used or, if the sensor offers the feature, the time set externally. TimestampStop MSGPACK int Acquisition time of the last beam of the scan in µs. The device's internal time base is used or, if the sensor offers the feature, the time set externally. ThetaStart MSGPACK int Azimuth angle of the first beam of the scan in radians. ThetaStop MSGPACK int Azimuth angle of the last beam of the scan in radians. ScanNumber MSGPACK int Not used. ModuleID MSGPACK int Number of the physical module that generated the data. In the case of the multiScan100, for example, this is one of the two measuring modules. ChannelTheta array of float32 Array of azimuth angles of a specific beam in radians. The encoding of the data in this array is described in "Serialization of arrays". The user can configure whether the array is present in the data structure. ChannelPhi array of float32 Array with the elevation angle of the scan in radians. Each Scan covers one layer, so this array contains one element. The encoding of the data in this array is described in "Serialization of arrays". The user can configure whether the array is present in the data structure. DistValues array of (array of float32) Array containing an array of distance values for each echo of the scan. The number of sub-arrays corresponds to the number of echoes in the scan, see also the EchoCount field below. The distance values are specified in mm. The encoding of the data in this array is described in "Serialization of arrays". The user can configure whether the array is present in the data structure. RssiValues array of (array of uint16) Array containing an array of RSSI values for each echo of the scan. The number of sub-arrays corresponds to the number of echoes in the scan, see also the EchoCount field below. For the representation of RSSI values, see RSSI scaling. The encoding of the data in this array is described in "Serialization of arrays". The user can configure whether the array is present in the data structure. PropertiesValues array of uint8 Array with additional properties, for example "reflector", for each beam of a scan. The encoding of the data in this array is described in "Serialization of arrays". This array is optional. BeamCount MSGPACK int Number of beams in the current scan. EchoCount MSGPACK int Number of echoes in the current scan.

For more details about the MSGPACK int format family, see the official msgpack specification.

DistValues and RssiValues array structure.

The diagram illustrates the nested array structure with 3 echoes and 15 beams, showing how each beam contains values for all echoes in both DistValues and RssiValues arrays.

docs.title: Serialization of Arrays
docs.text:
Arrays of measurement data (ChannelTheta, ChannelPhi, DistValues, RssiValues, and PropertiesValues) are encoded as follows:

msgpack_map_header {
  "numOfElems": <number of array elements>,
  "elemSz": <size of one array element in bytes>,
  "endian": little,
  "elemTypes": <typesArray>,
  "data": <binaryData>
}

The meaning of the individual fields of the Array class are shown in the following table.

Serialization of Arrays: name and description.

Name Description numOfElems Number of array elements elemSz Size of an array element in bytes, e.g., 4 for float32 or 1 for uint8. endian The value is always little elemTypes Array of element types. Only arrays with one element are supported here. Example: {float32} for an array of float32 values. An array of tuples would need multiple element types; such arrays are not used. data Actual payload. The data is encoded as a byte array in the MSGPACK format and can be copied directly into a structure/array after parsing the MSGPACK structure, taking into account the endianness and the data type.

docs.title: WebSocket Events
docs.text:
Compatible with: picoScan100

Instead of polling the REST API for state, you can open one persistent WebSocket connection, register the events you care about, and the device pushes a JSON frame every time a value changes. Use it for low-latency notifications: field-evaluation results, I/O switching, temperature alarms, firmware-update progress.

docs.title: Endpoint and Connection
docs.text:
ws://<device-ip>/apievents

Port 80 is used, and no authentication is required to open the connection. No periodic ping/keep-alive is needed. Every event has a matching REST endpoint of the same name; the data payload is identical to GET /api/<EventName>. Use REST for one-shot reads/writes, WebSocket for change notifications.

The device sends compressed frames (RSV1 = 1). Your WebSocket library must negotiate the permessage-deflate extension during the handshake, or the device closes the connection with protocol error 1002. Libraries that auto-negotiate (e.g. C++ httplib::WebSocketClient) work out of the box; Python's websocket-client does not do this by default, so use a library that negotiates it, or enable compression explicitly.

docs.title: Message Format
docs.text:
All messages are JSON text frames. Five types are used.

Register (client → device): one message per event, where clientId is a caller-chosen integer echoed back for that registration.

{ "type": "register", "event": "temperatureAlarmStatus", "clientId": 1 }

Registration confirmation (device → client): on success (status: 0) the device immediately sends the current value. Dispatch it exactly like a live event; it is your first data point.

{ "type": "register", "event": "temperatureAlarmStatus", "clientId": 1,
  "status": 0, "data": { "AlarmState": "NoAlarm" } }

Event push (device → client): sent whenever the value changes.

{ "type": "event", "event": "temperatureAlarmStatus", "clientId": 1,
  "status": 0, "data": { "AlarmState": "OverTemp" } }

Error (device → client): sent for an unknown or unavailable event. The connection stays open and other registrations are unaffected.

{ "type": "register", "event": "nonExistentEvent", "clientId": 2,
  "status": 1, "error": "Failed to register event ... Does the event exist?" }

Deregister (client → device): no response is sent.

{ "type": "deregister", "event": "temperatureAlarmStatus", "clientId": 1 }

docs.title: Step by Step
docs.text:
Send registration messages one at a time with at least 200 ms between consecutive frames. If several register frames arrive in a tight burst the device resets the connection. The delay is only needed during the initial registration sequence.

  1. Open the WebSocket to ws://<device-ip>/apievents (with permessage-deflate).
  2. Register your events, one register per event, unique clientId, at least 200 ms apart.
  3. Receive initial values: each successful registration replies with type: "register", status: 0, and the current value in data. Dispatch it like a live event.
  4. Handle events: keep reading; on change the device pushes type: "event".
  5. Handle errors and reconnect: log any status != 0; other registrations still work.

docs.title: Dispatch Pattern
docs.text:
Dispatch on both type and status so you also catch the initial value. The snippets are language-neutral pseudocode:

connection = websocket_connect(
    "ws://<device-ip>/apievents",
    compression="permessage-deflate",
)

for client_id, event_name in enumerate(events):
    connection.send({
        "type": "register",
        "event": event_name,
        "clientId": client_id,
    })
    sleep(milliseconds=200)

while connection.is_open():
    obj = json_parse(connection.receive())

    if obj["type"] == "event" or (
        obj["type"] == "register" and obj["status"] == 0
    ):
        dispatch(obj["event"], obj["data"])
    elif obj["type"] == "register" and obj["status"] != 0:
        log_error(obj["event"], obj["error"])

docs.title: Advanced: Throttle and Queue
docs.text:
Pass an optional options object when registering.

Throttle caps delivery frequency; excess events are dropped before queuing:

{ "type": "register", "event": "LSPdatetime", "clientId": 7,
  "options": { "throttle": { "minOutputIntervalMs": 5000 } } }

Queue means each event has its own per-event queue on the shared connection:

"options": { "queue": { "priority": "HIGH", "maxSize": 10, "discardIfFull": "OLDEST" } }

Advanced: Throttle and Queue: field, values, default, and meaning.

Field Values Default Meaning priority HIGH, MID, LOW MID Processing priority among events on this connection maxSize integer 1 Maximum buffered events discardIfFull OLDEST, NEWEST OLDEST Which event to drop when full

docs.title: Subscribable Events
docs.text:
Event names are case-sensitive. Full data schemas are in the OpenAPI spec under the matching GET endpoint.

Subscribable Events: event and typical trigger.

Event Typical trigger DeviceStatus Device operational state changes SCdevicestate Safety controller state FieldEvaluationResult Object enters/leaves a detection field perpendicularDistanceResult Perpendicular-distance result changes InputState / OutputState / PortState Digital I/O state changes (PortState preferred) ContaminationData / ContaminationResult Lens contamination per sector / global result InertialMeasurementUnit Live IMU data CurrentTempDev / temperatureAlarmStatus Temperature (°C) / alarm threshold crossed UpdateState Firmware-update progress LSPdatetime Device clock tick (every second)

docs.title: Test with Insomnia
docs.text:
Before wiring subscriptions into your app, verify them interactively. The video below shows how to open the connection, register an event, and receive WebSocket frames in Insomnia.

picoScan100: WebSocket Event API.

docs.title: Reliability and Reconnect
docs.text: The device may close the connection on network interruption or firmware restart, and no subscription state is preserved across connections. On a close event, wait, reconnect, and re-register every subscription.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Troubleshooting: symptom, likely cause, and fix.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Connection refused Wrong IP / not reachable Ping the device; check firewall Resets after first registration Register frames sent too fast ≥ 200 ms between register messages Closes immediately (error 1002) permessage-deflate not negotiated Use a library that negotiates it, or enable compression "Event not found" Wrong name (case-sensitive) or absent on this firmware Check the exact name; confirm firmware No events after registration Value hasn't changed; events are change-driven Expected; the initial value is still sent on registration Stale app state at startup Dispatch filter only accepts type == "event" Also dispatch type == "register" with status == 0 Frequent drops Read timeout too short Set read timeout ≥ 300 s; events can be infrequent

Test subscriptions from a plain browser (Chrome/Edge) or from Insomnia/Postman before wiring them into your app. Wireshark on the sensor interface shows the raw WebSocket traffic.

docs.title: 3D with 2D LiDARs
docs.text:
Compatible with: picoScan100

The picoScan100 measures distance and intensity in a single plane. Mounting it on a motorized axis (tilt, rotation, or a linear stage) sweeps that plane through 3D space. If an incremental encoder is attached to the axis, the rotation angle at the moment of each scan is known precisely. This means every 2D point can be rotated into a common 3D frame, and a full sweep becomes a dense 3D point cloud.

Two approaches exist. Choose based on where you want the geometry code to run.

3D with 2D LiDARs: comparison criterion, Approach A (host-side), and Approach B (on-device).

Approach A (host-side) Approach B (on-device) Angle source Encoder wired to the sensor Encoder wired to the sensor, or the built-in IMU Processing Host receives raw UDP frames and applies the 3D transform Device accumulates and saves a PCD file internally Result One host-generated .pcd per sweep Single .pcd from GET /cloud.pcd Best for Custom transforms, real-time streaming, maximum flexibility Simple integration, no host-side geometry code

For every scan frame, the sensor sends an encoder telegram (Compact type 4) with the same frame_number and the encoder tick count. This gives frame-accurate synchronization without timing jitter between the scan and position streams. Encoder input is available on the picoScan150.

docs.title: Hardware and Ports
docs.text:
A typical example is a sensor on a motorized tilt axis with a SICK DFS60-series incremental encoder wired to the sensor's encoder input. The same idea applies to rotation or linear stages: what matters is that an encoder on the moving axis feeds the sensor so each scan frame carries a position value.

Hardware and Ports: stream, protocol, port, and content.

Stream Protocol Port Content Scan data Compact UDP 2115 2D distance + intensity per segment, with frame_number Encoder data Compact UDP 7504 tick_count, reference ticks, speed, frame_number

Enable encoder data output (EncoderDataEnable, destination in EncoderDataEthSettings, default port 7504) and reset the encoder counter at the reference position before you collect data. The Configuration backup & restore flow is a convenient way to apply a validated encoder configuration.

docs.title: Synchronize by Frame Number
docs.text:
Both UDP streams carry a frame_number. Build a lookup table from that number to the encoder tick, so you can retrieve the exact axis angle for any scan frame even when the two streams arrive slightly out of order:

on encoder packet:  encoder_map[packet.frame_number] = packet.tick_count
on scan frame:      tick = encoder_map.lookup(frame.frame_number)  # or most-recent tick

Keep the table bounded in size to avoid unbounded memory growth over long acquisitions.

docs.title: Coordinate Transform
docs.text:
Convert each encoder tick to an angle, then rotate the 2D scan point around the axis. For a tilt axis along the world Y-axis with the scan plane horizontal at the reference:

theta   = (tick / ticks_per_revolution) * 2 * PI      # radians
x_world = x_scan * cos(theta)
y_world = y_scan                                       # lateral axis unchanged
z_world = x_scan * sin(theta)

Set ticks-per-revolution correctly. This value is specific to your encoder model. A mismatch produces a distorted point cloud. Reset the encoder counter at the reference position so tick 0 is your angular origin, and adapt the transform for a different axis orientation or a linear stage.

docs.title: End-to-End Pseudocode
docs.text:
Reset the encoder counter to establish tick 0:

POST /api/mResetEncoderIncrement

Process the two UDP streams and transform each scan frame:

encoder_map = {}          # frame_number -> tick
cloud_pts   = []

def on_encoder_packet(pkt):
    encoder_map[pkt.frame_number] = pkt.tick_count

def on_scan_frame(frame, points_2d):
    tick  = encoder_map.get(frame.frame_number, last_known_tick)
    theta = (tick / TICKS_PER_REV) * 2 * PI
    for (x, y, intensity) in points_2d:
        cloud_pts.append({ x: x*cos(theta), y: y, z: x*sin(theta), intensity })

udp_listen(port=2115, callback=on_scan_frame)
udp_listen(port=7504, callback=on_encoder_packet)
run_until_interrupted()
save_pcd(cloud_pts, "cloud.pcd")

The sick_perception_sdk (C++17) is a good starting point for a host-side implementation.

docs.title: Approach B: On-Device Scan Merger
docs.text:
The on-device scan merger runs entirely on the device. While the sensor rotates, it combines consecutive 2D profiles into a 3D point cloud and saves a .pcd file in device storage. The host only needs to trigger, poll, and download the result with one HTTP GET; no UDP parsing or transform code is required. The angle source is configurable (encoder, or the built-in IMU when no encoder is available).

Live capture of the 3D scan recording interface on a picoScan100.

docs.title: Configuration Parameters
docs.text:
Configuration Parameters: parameter, endpoint, values, and description.

Parameter Endpoint Values Description ScanMergerEnabled POST /api/ScanMergerEnabled true / false Enable the scan merger ScanMergerSource POST /api/ScanMergerSource 0 (IMU) / 1 (ENCODER) Rotation reference ScanMergeTrigger POST /api/ScanMergeTrigger 0 (METHOD) Start/stop via method calls RotationOffset POST /api/RotationOffset {x, y, z} in mm Sensor offset from the rotation axis

Setting parameters and calling merger methods requires challenge-response authentication.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Configure the merger parameters and persist them with WriteEeprom.
  2. POST /api/ResetScanMergeView: clear any previous recording.
  3. POST /api/StartScanMerge: start recording while the axis moves.
  4. POST /api/StopScanMerge: stop recording after the sweep.
  5. Poll GET /api/MergeSaving until it changes from true (saving) back to false. The point cloud is then ready.
  6. GET /cloud.pcd (port 80, outside /api/): download the point cloud, for example curl http://192.168.0.1/cloud.pcd -o cloud.pcd.

Only the most recent point cloud is available. The scan merger is a one-shot recorder: it accumulates on the device and stores one PCD file. There is no continuous 3D output. For continuous 3D, use Approach A or the Compact stream with your own accumulation.

docs.title: Cybersecurity
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Download the product-specific Cybersecurity Hardening Guide from Downloads on the individual product page at sick.com: LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, or picoScan100.

Cybersecurity covers the entire product life cycle. Increasing digitalization and network complexity in production plants increases the risk of cyberattacks from inside or outside the production network. A comprehensive cybersecurity strategy is therefore essential.

The asset owner is responsible for installing and maintaining security measures. Securing SICK devices in a network requires the active participation of the asset owner.

The recommendations below apply to the LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, and picoScan100. Menus, default states, available services, and authentication requirements vary by family, variant, and firmware. Sections with device-specific values name the products they cover. Confirm settings in the product-specific hardening guide and the device interface before applying them.

This page covers:

  • Communication security and access management
  • Application and field-evaluation aspects
  • User levels
  • Device interfaces
  • Ethernet-related settings

docs.title: Further Cybersecurity Information
docs.text:
For a cybersecurity overview, see SICK PSIRT. Current security advisories are listed on the SICK PSIRT Security Advisories page. Report security issues to the SICK Product Security Incident Response Team (SICK PSIRT). Read SICK's Information Handling Policies before sending security details.

Product-specific settings and telegram details are available from the device documentation. The product page is available through the SICK Product ID: pid.sick.com/{P/N}/{S/N}, where {P/N} is the part number and {S/N} is the serial number shown on the type label. The same part number links the device to its Asset Administration Shell, which holds the data sheet, operating instructions, certificates, and CAD data of the product type.

The examples and recommended settings on this page are general guidance, not customer-specific solutions or a replacement for specialist technical advice. Use the product-specific hardening guide and product documentation for the device and firmware in your installation.

docs.title: Intended Use
docs.text:
These are non-contact LiDAR sensors for indoor or outdoor, mobile or stationary use in stand-alone operation. LRS4000 and picoScan100 are 2D LiDAR families; multiScan100 and multiScan200 are multi-layer 3D LiDAR families. Depending on the device, configuration, and application software, typical applications include:

  • Continuous output of measurement data
  • Monitoring freely defined fields, with object detection signaled through digital outputs or telegrams
  • Stationary field protection, area monitoring, and access control
  • Navigation and anti-collision for mobile platforms
  • Profile detection, collision protection, object protection, and access monitoring
  • 3D mapping, environment perception, and volume monitoring (multiScan200)

Use the device only in industrial environments (EN 61000-6-4). Incorrect use, improper modification, or tampering invalidates any warranty and may result in damage for which SICK AG accepts no responsibility.

docs.title: Environmental Influences
docs.text: For outdoor variants, fog, steam, dust, rain, and snow can affect the detection range. The effect can only be quantified through a verification test at the intended site.

docs.title: Restrict Physical Access
docs.text: Operate the device in a protected area where only instructed and approved personnel have access.

docs.title: Limit Exposure to Public Networks
docs.text: Do not use the devices in public networks. Use an isolated network wherever possible to reduce exposure and risk.

docs.title: Establish an Update Strategy
docs.text:
Keep the device firmware up to date:

  1. Search for the product at sick.com.
  2. Check Downloads for the latest firmware version and release notes.
  3. Check for updates regularly and apply them as they become available.
  4. Test updates in the specific installation before deploying them at larger scale.

Perform firmware updates only in a trusted environment. Release notes contain information about included security patches.

docs.title: Configuration Backup and Restore
docs.text: Keep a protected backup of a known-working configuration so that the device can be returned to a secure state. The Backup & restore workflow supports multiScan100, multiScan200, and picoScan100. A passphrase can encrypt the backup. File-transfer authentication differs by firmware; follow the instructions for the matching OpenAPI file.

docs.title: Data Integrity
docs.text: Verify downloaded .spk and .sdd files with the instructions at sick.com/verify-downloads. The LFTchecksum workflow is available on multiScan200 and picoScan100.

docs.title: Brute-Force Protection
docs.text: After five consecutive unsuccessful login attempts, the picoScan100 enters a 30-second time lock. Do not assume the same threshold or lockout duration on other families; check their product-specific hardening guide.

docs.title: Periodic Security Tests
docs.text: Regularly verify that the security system works as intended and document the results.

docs.title: Device Identification
docs.text:
Verify that the correct device type and system plug are connected. The product ID uniquely identifies the device and consists of its part number and serial number. Find the product ID on the device and system-plug labels, or read it through the user interface.

The device information also shows the currently installed firmware version, which follows semantic versioning. The device part number can also be read through the API:

GET http://192.168.0.1/api/OrderNumber

Read the serial number with GET http://192.168.0.1/api/SerialNumber. Together they form the product ID pid.sick.com/{P/N}/{S/N}. See Link A Device To Its AAS to connect this ID with the product type data.

For telegram-based access, refer to the CoLa / LMDscandata documentation and the Compact format.

docs.title: Use the Device-Not-Ready Status
docs.text: The Device-Not-Ready status signals that the device is not operating correctly. Monitor it through communication or a digital output. A change to this state while device parameters are being changed can be used as a manipulation warning.

docs.title: Protection Levels
docs.text:
Each protection level assumes that the recommendations from the previous level are followed.

Protection Levels: protection level, intended use, and procedures.

Protection level Use for Procedures No protection Demonstrations or test scenarios Set factory defaults Basic protection Recommended minimum for daily operation in an uncritical environment Check firmware and release notes; change all passwords; configure network settings; disconnect unused interfaces; close unused ports and services Advanced protection Exposed or critical systems with advanced security requirements Apply basic protection and limit network access by IP range

docs.title: No Protection
docs.text: In this state there are no access restrictions: passwords remain at their defaults and interfaces are active. Do not use this state for daily operation. Use it only for demonstrations or tests, or when physical access is restricted and the device is isolated from the network or protected by a firewall.

docs.title: Set Factory Defaults
docs.text:
To start from a known state:

  1. Log in to the device with user level Service.
  2. Verify the user level.
  3. Set the device to factory defaults.

The device resets default passwords and reboots with the standard IP address 192.168.0.1. If a different IP address was previously used, either open the default address in a web browser or search for and reconnect to the device in SOPAS ET.

docs.title: Basic Protection
docs.text: Basic protection is the minimum recommended level for daily operation in an uncritical environment.

docs.title: Check Firmware and Release Notes
docs.text: Critical vulnerabilities can be discovered during the device life cycle. Updating firmware is therefore an important cybersecurity measure. Before commissioning, install the latest firmware and review its release notes for security patches. Update only in a trusted environment.

docs.title: Change Passwords
docs.text:
Enable only the user levels required by the deployment and assign each a unique, secret password. Factory user-level states vary by family and firmware. Follow the User levels guide for the current activation and password workflow.

Use passwords containing uppercase letters, lowercase letters, special characters, and numbers. Change passwords over a confidential connection, preferably a point-to-point connection during initial commissioning.

docs.title: Reset the Service Password (picoScan100)
docs.text:
On picoScan100, only the Service password can be reset to its default through the password-reset process:

  1. Select Password forgotten.
  2. Send the generated email to the responsible SICK sales company or service partner listed at sick.com/worldwide.
  3. Paste the received code and select Reset.

Selecting Cancel aborts the process. Request a new reset code from the manufacturer if necessary.

To regain access to another user level, first reset the Service password, back up the configuration, and then reset the device to factory defaults.

docs.title: Configure Network Settings
docs.text:
The documented factory network defaults for the device families covered here are:

Configure Network Settings: setting and default.

Setting Default IP address 192.168.0.1 Subnet mask 255.255.255.0 Default gateway 0.0.0.0

The following network-service defaults are for multiScan200 and picoScan100 only:

Configure Network Settings: service, port, multiScan200, and picoScan100.

Service Port multiScan200 picoScan100 HTTP (web server, REST) TCP 80 Enabled Enabled CoLa A / CoLa B TCP 2111 / 2112 Disabled Enabled CoLa2 TCP 2122 Disabled Always enabled Device search UDP 30718 Enabled Time-limited

LRS4000 and multiScan100 also provide a Diagnostics > Cybersecurity view with service and protocol information. Check that view on the target device; do not infer their defaults from the table above. The LRS4000 and multiScan100 walkthroughs show where to inspect these settings.

docs.title: Disconnect Unused Interfaces
docs.text: If a communication interface is not used by the application, disconnect its communication cable. For example, an application using only digital I/O does not need a permanently connected communication interface used only for parameterization.

docs.title: Close Unused Ports and Services
docs.text: Disable every protocol that is not required for operation. This reduces the device's attack surface.

docs.title: Legacy Protocols (CoLa)
docs.text: CoLa1 (CoLa ASCII/Binary) is a legacy interface for configuration and status requests. Disable it when the application does not need it. On multiScan200 and picoScan100, manage this service under Diagnostics > Cybersecurity; CoLa1 is disabled by default on multiScan200 and enabled by default on picoScan100. On LRS4000 and multiScan100, inspect the service state and available controls on the device before changing it.

docs.title: SOPAS ET Device Search
docs.text:
Limit device visibility through broadcast scanning. On picoScan100, the device search setting offers four modes:

SOPAS ET Device Search: mode and behavior.

Mode Behavior Enabled The device can be discovered and its IP address can be changed without authentication. Time-Limited The device can be discovered and its IP address can be changed without authentication for 60 seconds after boot. Restricted The device can be discovered, but its IP address cannot be edited without authentication. Disabled The device cannot be discovered. Recommended where applicable.

Device search uses UDP port 30718. It is Time-Limited by default on the picoScan100.

On the multiScan200, device search is enabled by default; disable it in Diagnostics > Cybersecurity when it is not required.

On LRS4000 and multiScan100, check the device's cybersecurity service list for the device-search service and its current state. The picoScan100 modes and default values above do not necessarily apply to those families.

docs.title: Web Server
docs.text: On multiScan200 and picoScan100, the web server uses TCP port 80 and is enabled by default. It provides browser-based visualization and parameterization; when disabled, the sensor remains reachable through SOPAS ET. For LRS4000 and multiScan100, inspect the cybersecurity service list and the product-specific hardening guide before disabling web access.

docs.title: CoLa2
docs.text: CoLa2 uses TCP port 2122. On picoScan100 it cannot be disabled. On multiScan200 it is disabled by default; enable it in Diagnostics > Cybersecurity only when required. Check the product-specific service list for CoLa2 availability on other families.

docs.title: Measurement Data Output
docs.text:
Enable measurement data output only when required:

  1. Log in as Authorized client.
  2. Open Application > Data output > Measurement data output.
  3. Enable UDP streaming.

Enabling measurement data output opens a device-side UDP port. Disabling it closes that port again.

docs.title: IMU Data Output
docs.text: Where supported by the device variant and licenses, configure IMU output under Application > Data output > IMU data output as Authorized client. Enable UDP streaming only when required. It opens a device-side UDP port; disabling the stream closes the port.

docs.title: Digital I/O
docs.text: Configure digital signals for device-specific application signals, such as DeviceNotReady or field evaluations, under Configuration > Inputs and outputs. Log in as Authorized client.

docs.title: Date and System Time
docs.text: Configure synchronized time under Basic settings > Date and system time as Authorized client, where this setting is available. NTP uses network time-server traffic. All four families support PTP over UDP ports 319 and 320. Check the device's service list and time-synchronization guide for supported methods and current state.

docs.title: User Levels
docs.text: On multiScan200 and picoScan100, only Service is enabled in the documented factory state; it cannot be deactivated. Factory user-level states can differ on LRS4000 and multiScan100. Check the User Levels guide and the product-specific hardening guide before enabling or disabling a level.

docs.title: Use Encrypted Communication
docs.text: Use HTTPS to encrypt web-interface and REST communication. Measurement data sent over UDP or TCP is not encrypted by HTTPS. Follow the HTTPS & certificates guide to upload a valid certificate bundle and verify the enabled state.

docs.title: Advanced Protection
docs.text: Advanced settings are applied in addition to the basic settings.

docs.title: Limit Network Access by IP Range
docs.text:
Change the default IP address to a non-default value and limit the subnet mask to the smallest subnet that meets the application's needs. Subnetting reduces broadcast traffic and makes it easier to isolate network problems.

Configure this under Configuration > Connection options > Ethernet as Service.

docs.title: Primary Sensor Data
docs.text: The supported data formats vary by family. Use the Data Streaming overview to choose a format available on the device and review its security implications. Measurement data sent over UDP or TCP is not encrypted by HTTPS. The notes below on telegram fields are limited to the named formats and families.

docs.title: Compact Format (Recommended)
docs.text:
Compact packets contain user data and a CRC32 checksum. Telegram headers and fields differ by format and family.

Type 1 scan telegrams are used by LRS4000, multiScan100, and picoScan100.

multiScan200 uses type 6 scan telegrams.

Consult the Compact format guide for the device-specific fields used to check data identity, ordering, timing, and integrity.

docs.title: MSGPACK Format (multiScan100 and picoScan100)
docs.text:
MSGPACK is available on multiScan100 and picoScan100. The following packet fields and segment details describe the documented picoScan100 structure; check the matching product documentation before relying on them for another family.

MSGPACK Format (multiScan100 and picoScan100): field and purpose.

Field Purpose Telegram counter Counts measurement-data telegrams since power-up, starting at 1; detects lost data. Transmit timestamp Sensor system time in microseconds since 1970-01-01 00:00 UTC; detects delays. Synchronize the sensor with a time server where required. Segment counter Identifies segments. A 276° frame is split into 10 segments of 30° or 5 segments of 60°, depending on the scanning frequency. Frame number Counts frames since device startup; detects lost data. Sender ID Contains the device serial number; identifies the sending sensor. CRC32 checksum Follows the user data and is calculated over the MSGPACK buffer only, without the STX bytes and the size field.

docs.title: LMDscandata Format (LRS4000, multiScan100, and picoScan100)
docs.text:
LMDscandata is available on LRS4000, multiScan100, and picoScan100. The following field details describe the documented picoScan100 structure; check the product-specific telegram listing for another family:

LMDscandata Format (LRS4000, multiScan100, and picoScan100): field and purpose.

Field Purpose Serial number Identifies the sending device. Telegram counter Counts telegrams created since power-up, starting at 1; detects lost data. Version number Identifies the serialization version and helps trace structure changes. Scan counter Counts scans actually created by the device. Time since startup Counts microseconds since power-up, starting at 0. Device time Sensor system time since 1970-01-01 00:00 UTC in microseconds; detects delays. XOR checksum Verifies transfer integrity. CoLa B only: one byte, the XOR of all data bytes.

docs.title: Secondary Sensor Data
docs.text:
multiScan100 and picoScan100 use Compact type 2 for IMU data. multiScan200 uses type 7, with its standard header. The LRS4000 provides IMU data through CoLa events or the REST API instead of Compact. Use the Compact format guide for device-specific IMU fields:

  • Telegram version: the described telegram structure uses version 1.
  • IMU sensor timestamp: sensor system time in µs since 1970-01-01 00:00 UTC; detects delays in the data stream.
  • CRC32 checksum: CRC32 of all words except the checksum.

docs.title: Device State
docs.text:
Monitor device state to detect changes in parameterization:

  • CoLa sRN SCdevicestate transmits the general device state.
  • REST GET /api/DeviceStatus reads the device status.

docs.title: Last Modified Information
docs.text: Protect and monitor the information about when device parameters were changed and stored. Find it under Diagnosis > Overview > Operating information.

docs.title: Messages
docs.text: Regularly review the diagnostic overview under Diagnosis > Overview > Messages. If the sensor is not working as intended, use the troubleshooting information to correct the problem or determine how to proceed.

docs.title: Diagnostic File
docs.text:
The device provides a diagnostic file for in-depth analysis. Only SICK can read this file. Use NTP synchronization so that device information can be assigned correctly:

  1. Log in as Service.
  2. Open Basic settings > Date and system time and configure NTP or PTP.
  3. Open Diagnostics > Overview > Diagnostic file.
  4. Select Create file, then download the file.

docs.title: Changing Parameters
docs.text: Prevent unauthorized operators from changing parameters because parameter changes can alter application results. Limit access to device parameters to the minimum number of people required by the need-to-know principle.

docs.title: MATLAB Integration
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan200 picoScan100

MATLAB ROS Toolbox can subscribe directly to native ROS 2 data from multiScan200 or picoScan100 through DDS. No SICK ROS driver or bridge is required. The example below uses picoScan100 point-cloud data on /cloud/all_points as sensor_msgs/PointCloud2 with the default ROS domain ID 0.

docs.title: Validated Setup
docs.text:
Validated Setup: component and version or setting.

Component Version / setting Operating system Windows 11 MATLAB R2025b with ROS Toolbox ROS 2 / DDS Kilted with CycloneDDS ROS domain ID 0 (device default)

All DDS participants must use the same domain ID as the sensor. Ensure that the sensor's native ROS 2 interface is enabled and that the computer firewall allows DDS traffic. See Native ROS 2 for sensor-side setup.

docs.title: Receive PointCloud2 Data
docs.text:
The following script creates a MATLAB ROS 2 node, lists visible topics, and prints the number of points received on /cloud/all_points.

node = ros2node("/matlab_cloud_counter");

disp("Available ROS 2 topics:");
disp(ros2("topic", "list"));

sub = ros2subscriber( ...
    node, ...
    "/cloud/all_points", ...
    "sensor_msgs/PointCloud2", ...
    @onPointCloud);

disp("Subscribed to /cloud/all_points");

t0 = tic;
while toc(t0) < 10
    pause(0.1);
end

clear sub node
disp("Finished.");

function onPointCloud(msg)
    pointCount = double(msg.width) * double(msg.height);
    fprintf("PointCloud received: %d points\n", pointCount);
end

docs.title: Visualize Live Data
docs.text: Open Apps > ROS 2 Data Analyzer, choose Open > Live Network Data, select Live ROS 2 network data, and set the ROS domain ID to 0. Create a PointCloud Visualizer, choose /cloud/all_points, then select Start.

docs.title: Verify Connectivity
docs.text:
Use the ROS 2 CLI independently of MATLAB to verify that DDS data is present:

ros2 topic echo /cloud/all_points

If no data is visible, confirm the native ROS 2 interface configuration, firewall rules, DDS compatibility, and ROS domain ID. On multiScan200 and on picoScan100 from firmware V2.3.1, the sensor domain ID is configurable (rosDomainId); make sure MATLAB uses the same value.

docs.title: Milestone XProtect Camera Plugin
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Use Milestone XProtect to display camera video beside LiDAR events. Obtain the camera-specific SICK/Milestone package from the applicable download page: LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, or picoScan100. Look under software or integration downloads. If no package is listed, contact SICK support. Confirm that the package supports your XProtect release.

Milestone MIP SDK documentation explains the underlying plug-in deployment model.

docs.title: Model Context
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

When developing an application for a SICK LiDAR sensor, you can clone the relevant documentation or code repository into your project workspace. A local copy gives your coding assistant access to the repository's examples, configuration files, API usage, and implementation details while you work.

Clone the SICK LiDAR Developer Guide repository alongside your application:

git clone https://github.com/SICKAG/sick_lidar_developer_guide.git

Keep the clone up-to-date when you need the latest context:

git -C sick_lidar_developer_guide pull

This repository-based approach provides source context for your development tools. It is not an MCP server and does not expose an MCP tool or service.

docs.title: PLC Integration
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Use the CoLa command protocol over a TCP/IP socket to receive measurement, field-evaluation, and I/O data from SICK LiDAR sensors on Siemens, Beckhoff, Mitsubishi, or Rockwell PLCs. SICK does not provide maintained PLC function blocks for the product families on this page; implement a small length-prefixed receive routine using the controller's native TCP socket API.

docs.title: Interface and Approach
docs.text:
For PLC applications, use CoLa B on TCP port 2112. Its length-prefixed telegrams are easier to process than CoLa A on port 2111. Open one bidirectional TCP connection from the PLC to the sensor, keep it open, and poll the required values by sending an sRN request and reading the matching sRA response on that same connection.

Interface and Approach: interface, transport, and suitable use.

Interface Transport Suitable use CoLa A / B TCP 2111 / 2112 PLC commands and telegram access Compact / MSGPACK UDP High-rate scan streams to a computer or edge device REST API HTTP(S) 80 / 443 Configuration, diagnostics, and firmware updates

Configure the sensor once through SOPASair: use a fixed IP address reachable from the PLC, configure scan profiles, field-evaluation groups, and I/O, then export a parameter backup. Do not repeatedly configure the sensor from cyclic PLC logic. Enable LMDscandata only when the PLC requires distance data.

docs.title: Polling and CoLa B Framing
docs.text:
The PLC is the client and connects to <device-ip>:2112. Send a request, receive one complete telegram, parse it, and reconnect after an error or timeout.

connect(device_ip, 2112)
loop:
  send(frame("sRN LMDscandata"))
  reply = receive_one_telegram()
  parse(reply)

Every CoLa B telegram has this layout:

Polling and CoLa B Framing: field, size, and value.

Field Size Value Start 4 bytes 02 02 02 02 Length 4 bytes Big-endian payload length Payload N bytes Command type, name, and data Checksum 1 byte XOR of all payload bytes

TCP is a byte stream: a receive operation can return a partial telegram or several telegrams. Buffer incoming bytes; after at least eight bytes are available, validate the start sequence, read the big-endian length, then wait for exactly 8 + length + 1 bytes. Validate the XOR checksum, consume one telegram, and retain any remaining bytes for the next call.

docs.title: Common Telegrams
docs.text:
Common Telegrams: telegram, purpose, and PLC consideration.

Telegram Purpose PLC consideration SCdevicestate Device health Poll slowly and invalidate dependent values when not ready. LMDscandata Distance and optional RSSI data Reduce it below the network MTU where possible. perpendicularDistanceResult Minimum and maximum distance to a field boundary where the device supports perpendicular distance Its value can remain unchanged after the field is clear; gate it with field state. FieldEvaluationResult Free/occupied result for each evaluation group Map each group index to the configured physical zone. LIDinputstate / LIDoutputstate Digital I/O states Use to mirror sensor I/O in the PLC process image.

Request each with sRN <name> and parse the sRA <name> ... response. Confirm the exact payload layout, byte offsets, and data types against the Telegram Listing for the installed firmware.

To keep LMDscandata manageable, use only the required echo, disable RSSI when not needed, restrict the scan angle, and select the coarsest acceptable angular resolution. A small telegram reduces PLC processing load and TCP segmentation.

docs.title: Controller Notes
docs.text:
Controller Notes: controller and TCP mechanism.

Controller TCP mechanism Siemens S7-1500 / S7-1200 Open User Communication: TCON_IP_v4, TSEND_C, and TRCV_C; use variable-length receives. Siemens S7-300 / S7-400 CP module with AG_SEND / AG_RECV and FB54 TCP. Beckhoff TwinCAT 3 Tc2_TcpIp: FB_SocketConnect, FB_SocketSend, and FB_SocketReceive. Mitsubishi GX Works2 / iQ Ethernet socket services: SP_SOCOPEN, SP_SOCSND, SP_SOCRCV, and SP_SOCCLOSE. Rockwell / Allen-Bradley Raw TCP socket object with MSG instructions for connect, write, read, and close.

The transport API differs, but the CoLa B framing and receive-buffer logic are identical for every PLC.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Troubleshooting: symptom, cause, and action.

Symptom Cause Action Connection refused on 2112 Incorrect network settings or CoLa B disabled Verify the sensor IP/subnet and CoLa B configuration. No response Malformed request or wrong telegram name Validate start bytes, length, XOR checksum, and case-sensitive command name. sFA error response Unsupported or unavailable variable Check the CoLa error codes, Telegram Listing, and firmware version. Receive never completes Fixed-size receive or TCP fragmentation Buffer data and use the length field to determine the complete frame. Misaligned data Concatenated frames or unconsumed bytes Consume exactly one frame and retain the buffer remainder. Frozen values Repeated scan or stale perpendicular-distance result Verify scan counter/timestamp and use FieldEvaluationResult to validate the distance.

docs.title: Programming Tools and Examples
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Ready-made code for integrating SICK LiDAR sensors, published on GitHub (SICKAG). Use it as a starting point for receiving measurement data and controlling the sensor from your application. Check that a project supports your sensor firmware version (shown on the SOPASair Home page) before you start.

Programming Tools and Examples: language, project, use it for, technologies used, and compatible with.

Language Project Use it for Technologies used Compatible with C++ sick_perception_sdk C++17 SDK: connect, configure, run diagnostics, and receive the Compact stream; includes worked examples. A strong starting point for custom applications. REST with challenge-response authentication, HTTPS, Compact scan, IMU, and encoder telegrams (Type 4), UDP unicast and multicast, TCP, PCD export LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, picoScan100 C++ sick_scan_xd Generic C/C++ API of the sick_scan_xd driver: receive point clouds without ROS on Linux and Windows. CoLa over TCP for setup, Compact or MSGPACK over UDP (multiScan100, picoScan100), LMDscandata over CoLa B (LRS4000), IMU LRS4000, multiScan100, picoScan100 Python sick_scan_rest_client Scripted REST configuration with challenge-response handled for you. REST, challenge-response authentication (SHA-256 with salt), REST password change (AES-128, HMAC), CoLa A/B password hash multiScan200, picoScan100 Python sick_scan_xd Python API of the sick_scan_xd driver: receive point clouds without ROS on Linux and Windows. CoLa over TCP for setup, Compact or MSGPACK over UDP (multiScan100, picoScan100), LMDscandata over CoLa B (LRS4000), IMU LRS4000, multiScan100, picoScan100 Python ScanSegmentAPI Receive and analyze segmented scan data, for example plot it with matplotlib or record it to JSON. Compact (telegram type 1), MSGPACK, UDP, TCP, JSON export LRS4000, multiScan100, picoScan100 Python ScanSegmentDecoding Receive and decode MSGPACK scan segments without the full API. MSGPACK, UDP multiScan100, picoScan100 C# ScanSegmentAPICSharp Compact-format deserializer for .NET, with a worked example for receiving segmented scan data. Compact, UDP, .NET multiScan100, picoScan100

For MATLAB, see MATLAB Integration. To parse the Compact format in any other language, use the Kaitai Struct definitions.

For the REST API, start with the shared REST Interface guide. The complete, device-specific endpoint definitions are available in the LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, and picoScan100 OpenAPI references.

docs.title: ROS Integration
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

There are two ways to get LiDAR data into ROS 2: the sensor publishes ROS 2 messages itself (native ROS 2), or a driver on the host receives sensor data and publishes the messages (sick_scan_xd). Both deliver standard ROS 2 messages to your nodes. The difference is which product families they cover and where decoding and publishing run.

ROS Integration: integration path and compatible devices.

Integration path Compatible with Native ROS 2 multiScan200, picoScan100 sick_scan_xd LRS4000, multiScan100, picoScan100

The LRS4000 and multiScan100 do not support native ROS 2. Use sick_scan_xd for these families.

ROS 2 with sick_scan_xd The sensor sends data to the sick_scan_xd driver on the host, which publishes to customer ROS nodes 1 to N over DDS. LiDAR sensor Streaming App ROS 2 sick_scan_xd host driver Customer ROS Node 1 Customer ROS Node 2 Customer ROS Node N Native ROS 2 The native ROS 2 publisher on the sensor sends data over DDS directly to customer ROS nodes 1 to N, without a driver. Uses CycloneDDS as the ROS middleware. LiDAR sensor Streaming App ROS 2 Native ROS 2* Customer ROS Node 1 Customer ROS Node 2 Customer ROS Node N Protocol: driver-supported sensor data Protocol: DDS (Data Distribution Service) via UDP/IP * Native ROS 2 uses CycloneDDS as its ROS middleware (RMW).

ROS Integration: option, what it is, advantages, trade-offs, and best fit.

Option What it is Advantages Trade-offs Best fit Native ROS 2 The sensor firmware assembles the scan segments and publishes ROS 2 messages over DDS. No driver on the host; lower host CPU load; hardware timestamps; any number of subscribers and other DDS clients can receive the data directly. Cyclone DDS is the specified middleware; uses more network bandwidth than Compact; no IMU or diagnostics topics; configuration stays outside ROS 2; the picoScan150 needs a license. ROS 2 systems where host CPU matters, for example navigation or SLAM on embedded computers. sick_scan_xd A ROS 2 driver on the host receives data through the driver-supported sensor protocol, assembles the scans, and publishes the messages. Publishes PointCloud2, LaserScan, and IMU messages where supported; decoding is under host-side control; supports recording to rosbag files. Decoding and publishing use host CPU; the driver must be installed and maintained on the host. Applications that need IMU topics, LRS4000 or multiScan100 integration, or host-side control over decoding.

docs.title: Native ROS 2
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan200 picoScan100

The product supports native ROS 2 communication via the DDS (Data Distribution Service) protocol. This enables efficient real-time transmission of measured data without additional drivers and with minimum delay time. The data is output directly in ROS 2-compatible formats.

Note:

  • Filter settings in the product have a direct effect on the published data.
  • Subscribed topics are published even if no measurement points are available. It is therefore recommended that you only subscribe to required topics.
  • If the static IP address is changed, a restart of the device is required to output the topics correctly.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
1. Verify the ROS 2 with middleware Cyclone DDS is installed. Install the Eclipse Cyclone DDS middleware using the Cyclone DDS installation instructions.
  2. Enable Native ROS 2 (DDS) in the device web interface, open Application → Data output and set Measurement data output format to Native ROS 2 (DDS).
  3. Configure Cyclone DDS with the IP address of the host interface connected to the sensor.
  4. Start rviz2 and add one of the published topics.

The picoScan150 requires firmware V2.2.1 or later and an activated native ROS 2 license (PICOSCAN RosConnect). picoScan150 PRO versions (part numbers 1134610 and 1142273) are delivered with this license pre-installed. If the license is missing, contact SICK. See LiDAR License Activation for the official activation instructions.

The picoScan120 requires firmware V2.2.1 or later. The latest firmware and update instructions for both devices are available from the SICK firmware download.

picoScan150 native ROS 2 license.

On Windows, DDS discovery requires the sensor network interface to allow local network traffic. In PowerShell, inspect the interface and set it to Private if necessary. Replace 5 with the interface index connected to the sensor:

Get-NetConnectionProfile
Set-NetConnectionProfile -InterfaceIndex 5 -NetworkCategory Private

The ROS 2 domain ID on the host (ROS_DOMAIN_ID) must match the device. The default is 0; it can be changed with rosDomainId (0-232) or in SOPASair (multiScan200; picoScan100 from firmware V2.3.1). DDS/RTPS discovery must be able to reach the sensor interface. Native ROS 2 publishes data only; configure the sensor through the REST API, CoLa, or the web interface.

docs.title: Visualize the Point Cloud
docs.text:
Create a Cyclone DDS configuration file and set NetworkInterfaceAddress to the IP address of the host interface connected to the sensor. This example uses 192.168.0.100. See the Cyclone DDS configuration reference for additional options.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<CycloneDDS
  xmlns="https://cdds.io/config"
  xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
  xsi:schemaLocation="https://cdds.io/config https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eclipse-cyclonedds/cyclonedds/master/etc/cyclonedds.xsd">
  <Domain>
    <General>
      <NetworkInterfaceAddress>192.168.0.100</NetworkInterfaceAddress>
    </General>
  </Domain>
</CycloneDDS>
LinuxWindows

Source ROS 2, select Cyclone DDS, set the configuration file, and start rviz2:

. ~/ros2_humble/install/local_setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_cyclonedds_cpp
export CYCLONEDDS_URI="file://$HOME/CycloneDDS/my-config.xml"
rviz2

In rviz2, add /cloud/all_points or a scan topic. Set Fixed Frame to world, or to the frame configured on the device.

In a Windows command prompt, source ROS 2, select Cyclone DDS, set the configuration file, and start rviz2:

call C:\dev\ros2_humble\local_setup.bat
set RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_cyclonedds_cpp
set CYCLONEDDS_URI=file://%USERPROFILE%/cyclonedds.xml
rviz2

In rviz2, add /cloud/all_points or a scan topic. Set Fixed Frame to world, or to the frame configured on the device.

docs.title: Limitations and Trade-Offs
docs.text:
Native ROS 2 is a sensor-to-host data publisher, not a complete ROS 2 control interface:

  • No ROS diagnostics topic: Device health and diagnosis are not exposed as a diagnostics topic in the ROS 2 graph. Use the device web interface for diagnosis and troubleshooting. See the SOPASair overview.
  • Configuration stays outside ROS 2: The interface does not expose sensor parameters, services, or actions. Configure scan profiles, field of view, filters, and other device settings through the web interface, REST API, or CoLa; they cannot be set as ROS parameters or from a ROS 2 launch file.
  • Use CycloneDDS: Native ROS 2 is specified for CycloneDDS as the ROS middleware (RMW) on the host. Other RMW implementations, such as Fast DDS or Zenoh, and custom DDS environments are not validated. If you use one, test discovery and communication with your device firmware and ROS distribution.
  • Account for network load: Native ROS 2 uses more network bandwidth than Compact over UDP. The device publishes its available ROS topics concurrently, and topics can continue to be published when a scan contains no measurement points. Subscribe only to topics the application needs, monitor network utilization at the selected scan configuration, and consider Compact if bandwidth is constrained.
  • Publisher changes follow firmware releases: The DDS publisher runs in the sensor firmware, rather than a host-side driver. Publisher fixes and feature changes therefore depend on a firmware release.

docs.title: Published Topics
docs.text:
The native publisher exposes these topics simultaneously. All messages carry the hardware PTP timestamp in header.stamp. The rt prefix is the DDS-level name: in ROS 2 tools, rt<namespace>/cloud/all_points appears as <namespace>/cloud/all_points, for example /cloud/all_points.

The multiScan200 and picoScan100 publish the same PointCloud2 and LaserScan topics. The multiScan200 also publishes the ambient_light and imu topics, and a PointCloud2 topic per segment and echo.

PointCloud2 topics

Published Topics: PointCloud2 topic, contents ¹⁾, output frequency, and description.

PointCloud2 topic Contents ¹⁾ Output frequency Description rt<namespace>/cloud/all_points x,y,z,i,p Scan rate Valid scan points of all segments and all echoes rt<namespace>/cloud/all_points_echo0 x,y,z,i,p Scan rate Valid scan points of echo 0 rt<namespace>/cloud/all_points_echo1 x,y,z,i,p Scan rate Valid scan points of echo 1 (only available if multi-echo is configured) rt<namespace>/cloud/all_points_echo2 x,y,z,i,p Scan rate Valid scan points of echo 2 (only available if multi-echo is configured) rt<namespace>/cloud/reflector_points x,y,z,i,p Scan rate Valid scan points that were recognized as reflectors rt<namespace>/cloud/segment[s] x,y,z,i,p Segment frequency Valid scan points of a selected segment s (only available for segments that are available after application of the angle range filter) rt<namespace>/cloud/segment[s]_echo[e] x,y,z,i,p Segment frequency multiScan200 only: valid scan points of echo e in segment s (only available for segments that are available after application of the angle range filter and depending on the configuration of the echo filter)

¹⁾ intensity (i): RSSI with value range: 0.0 ... 1.0; properties (p): Bit mask 0b00000001 indicates whether this measurement point was recognized as a reflection. On the multiScan200, sWN rosPointCloud2Content selects the optional channels RSSI, properties, time offset, and ring (layer index); see the multiScan200 CoLa Telegram Listing.
