docs.title: sick_perception_sdk
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

The sick_perception_sdk is a C++17 library for receiving SICK LiDAR data, configuring sensors, and building diagnostic or recording applications. It provides event-driven, thread-safe data acquisition from multiple sensors, as well as ready-to-use examples.

sick_perception_sdk data streaming, REST-based configuration, and additional tools.

docs.title: Supported Devices and Platforms
docs.text:
The SDK supports these device variants:

Supported Devices and Platforms: product family and variants.

Product family Variants LRS4000 LRS4581 multiScan100 multiScan136, multiScan165, multiScan166 multiScan200 multiScan270 picoScan100 picoScan120, picoScan150

The SDK's example build option targets LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, or picoScan100.

The project builds with CMake on Linux and Windows and supports x86_64 and ARM64. Tested platforms are Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, and Windows 11. macOS is not a tested platform.

docs.title: Build and Integrate
docs.text: The SDK uses CMake and Conan 2 is available for dependency management. Follow the upstream build instructions and CMake integration example for the current options and dependencies. The example build can be selected for a device family, and the CMake project exposes separate components for drivers, sensor configuration, and Compact format.

docs.title: Receive and Record Data
docs.text:
The SDK receives event-driven scan, IMU, and encoder data using SICK's Compact format over TCP or UDP. Scan data is exposed as point clouds (Public PointField::DataType API).

The Compact-format layer provides a PointCloudToPCDConverter helper for converting scan-derived point clouds to PCD for tools such as CloudCompare. This is a conversion facility. The SDK does not provide a separate, ready-made recording workflow. The sensor_configuration component provides REST-based access to sensor settings and status.

docs.title: Threading, Diagnostics, and Logging
docs.text:
Data acquisition is thread-safe and event-driven, including when acquiring from multiple sensors. The SDK includes diagnostic examples and built-in diagnostic and logging capabilities. The default logger uses plog; applications can provide a custom logger and set a minimum log level.

See the SDK README for current setup details, examples, and API documentation.

docs.title: SOPASair Recorder | .sc
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 picoScan100

The SOPASair Data recorder captures real LiDAR measurement data to a recording file (.sc) for later analysis and replay. A repeatable scene helps investigate unexpected detections or missed objects, compare application behavior after changes, and share the same measurement scenario with development or support teams.

docs.title: Open the Data Recorder
docs.text:
In the sensor's SOPASair web interface, open Diagnostics → Data recorder. The page provides an installation file for a separate recorder application:

  1. Download the data recorder installation file from SOPASair.
  2. Unzip the downloaded ZIP file and run the EXE.
  3. In the Connection Wizard, connect the recorder to the device. The recorder interface opens in a new window.
  4. Use the recorder application to capture the measurement scenario and save the .sc recording for later use.

The picoScan100 SOPASair Data recorder page links to the separate recorder application.

docs.title: When to Use It
docs.text:
• Capture a real scene during operation to investigate an intermittent issue.
  • Replay a captured measurement scenario to compare processing results across application changes, rather than returning to the installation site.
  • Share a recording with colleagues or SICK support for reproducible analysis.

Recordings capture a particular measurement scenario, not an entire device configuration or raw Ethernet traffic. Save the relevant configuration and firmware details separately when comparing behavior after changes. For a complete device configuration, use Backup & Restore; for raw network traffic, use Wireshark | pcap.

This is the SOPASair Data recorder workflow, not the separate legacy SOPAS ET Excel/CSV recording workflow. The availability of the recorder and replay functions may depend on device and software version; the illustrated entry point is from picoScan100. LRS4000 and multiScan100 also provide the SOPASair Diagnostics → Data recorder entry.

docs.title: Wireshark | pcap
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Packet captures record the raw Ethernet communication between the sensor and a host computer. Use Wireshark, tcpdump, or tshark to capture packets. A capture retains complete raw sensor data for protocol-level diagnostics. It is useful for customer support, network troubleshooting, and protocol decoder development. Captures are saved as .pcap or .pcapng files.

For Compact format captures, use the Wireshark Compact dissector to decode the packets. The Lua plug-in is available at COMPACT_Dissector.lua.

Wireshark displaying decoded Compact measurement data with the SICK dissector.

docs.title: Asset Administration Shell
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

The Asset Administration Shell (AAS) is the standardized digital twin of Industry 4.0. SICK publishes an AAS for each product part number at aas.sick.com. Access requires a SICK ID login. The AAS describes the product type in a machine-readable format, which makes it useful for engineering tools and asset management systems.

docs.title: What to Expect
docs.text:
• Nameplate: manufacturer, product designation, order code, and markings such as CE and UKCA
  • Technical data: product classification (ECLASS, ETIM) and key technical properties
  • Documents: data sheet, operating instructions, dimensional drawing, and certificates
  • CAD data: 3D models such as STEP files and the EPLAN macro
  • Contact information: SICK sales and service contacts

The AAS describes the part number, not an individual device. Serial number, firmware version, configuration, status, and measurement data come from the device itself through the REST API, the CoLa interface, and the data streams.

docs.title: Link a Device to Its AAS
docs.text: Each device is identified by its product ID pid.sick.com/{P/N}/{S/N}, made of the part number and the serial number from the type label. Both values can also be read from the device over the REST API. The part number connects the device to its AAS.

docs.title: Checksums
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan200 picoScan100

The LFTchecksum is a read-only REST resource that returns MD5 digests over four independent software and configuration areas of the device. It lets you verify at any time that nothing has changed since a known-good reference: detect unintended parameter changes, confirm a configuration file applied correctly, or check that a firmware update touched only the areas it should.

docs.title: Reading It
docs.text:
No authentication required:

GET /api/LFTchecksum

{
  "header": { "status": 0, "message": "Ok" },
  "data": { "LFTchecksum": {
    "MD5SumOK":       true,
    "MD5LinuxRoot":   "8439a3f5bb209f3d51557d509169ec60",
    "MD5App":         "304f9a18302e2b635da2c2c220463119",
    "MD5Calibration": "bc5e5d5df638dc45c85937c8c67b59d7",
    "MD5Parameters":  "07f18c8032e24ac65ca0ed7c04be6a62"
  } }
}

docs.title: The Four Sub-Checksums
docs.text:
The Four Sub-Checksums: field, covers, and changes when….

Field Covers Changes when… MD5LinuxRoot Linux root filesystem (OS layer) A firmware update modifies the OS partition MD5App Application binary and libraries A firmware update installs a new application version MD5Calibration Factory calibration data Calibration is recalculated/overwritten (factory service only) MD5Parameters Persistent parameter set (EEPROM) Parameters are persisted via WriteEeprom, or a config file is imported and persisted MD5SumOK Overall integrity flag false if any of the four fails its internal verification

docs.title: RAM vs. Persistent Storage
docs.text:
The device keeps two parameter states at once:

RAM vs. Persistent Storage: parameter state, storage location, persistence after reboot, and effect on MD5Parameters.

State Where Survives reboot? Reflected in MD5Parameters? Working copy RAM No (a RebootDevice flushes RAM to EEPROM first, so it survives a software reboot) No, until WriteEeprom or RebootDevice Persisted copy EEPROM / flash Yes Yes

Every REST write modifies only the RAM copy. MD5Parameters (the persisted digest) does not change until WriteEeprom is called, or the device is rebooted via RebootDevice (which persists RAM first). A SoftReset or a hard power-cycle discards unsaved RAM changes.

After a REST write, reading an unchanged MD5Parameters means the change is still in RAM only, not that the device is unmodified. Persist with WriteEeprom (or reboot) to make the change durable and visible in the checksum.

docs.title: When Does Each Sub-Checksum Change?
docs.text:
The following table shows the behavior of a picoScan150 (● = changed, - = unchanged):

When Does Each Sub-Checksum Change? Scenario and resulting change of the LinuxRoot, app, calibration, and parameters checksums.

Scenario LinuxRoot App Calibration Parameters Two consecutive reads, no operation - - - - Change a parameter in RAM only (no WriteEeprom) - - - - Change in RAM, then SoftReset - - - - Change in RAM, then RebootDevice (persists first) - - - ● Change + WriteEeprom - - - ● CreateParameterBackup → RestoreParameterBackup, same file, no content change - - - - LoadApplicationDefaults (destructive) - - - ● Firmware upgrade ● ● - - Firmware downgrade ● ● - -

MD5Calibration does not change through normal end-user operations. A change there indicates a factory calibration update or an unexpected write to the calibration partition, so treat it as a red flag.

docs.title: A Practical Integrity Workflow
docs.text:
1. Record all four hashes from a known-good device (the reference).
  2. After any change (a config push, a restore, a firmware update), read LFTchecksum again.
  3. Compare field by field: a firmware update should move MD5LinuxRoot + MD5App only; a persisted config change should move MD5Parameters only; MD5Calibration should never move.
  4. Anything else is unexpected: investigate before putting the device back into service.

Compact and MSGPACK telegrams carry a CRC32 per packet (see Compact Format); CoLa B telegrams carry a 1-byte XOR checksum. The LFTchecksum covers the stored software and configuration, which complements these on-the-wire checks.

docs.title: Device Discovery
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

This page explains the available discovery methods for locating a SICK LiDAR sensor on the network. Use the method that best fits your commissioning environment to find the device address quickly.

There are three ways to find a sensor:

  1. Use the default IP for a direct first connection.
  2. Use SOPAS ET network search when the sensor is already connected to a local network.
  3. Implement discovery yourself when discovery must be part of an application or provisioning workflow.

docs.title: Default IP
docs.text:
For a direct first connection, connect the sensor to the computer with Ethernet and use the factory default IP address:

Default IP: parameter and value.

Parameter Value Sensor IP address 192.168.0.1 Subnet mask 255.255.255.0

Set the computer's Ethernet adapter to a different address in the same subnet, for example 192.168.0.100, then open http://192.168.0.1/ in a browser. See Getting started for the Windows procedure.

docs.title: SOPAS ET Network Search
docs.text:
SOPAS ET provides a graphical network search for SICK devices. Connect the sensor to the same Ethernet segment as the computer and start the search. The result lists responsive devices with their IP address, MAC address, and device identity.

SOPAS ET network search showing a discovered picoScan device.

Use this approach when the sensor is already connected to a switch or when its configured address is unknown. The search uses the same local broadcast principle as the protocol described below; it does not cross routers.

docs.title: Your Own Implementation
docs.text:
SICK devices answer a UDP broadcast discovery telegram, so a host on the same segment can locate every device without knowing its address in advance. This requires no authentication and no REST call: send one broadcast datagram to 255.255.255.255:30718; every responsive device replies by unicast with its full network configuration.

This is a limited broadcast: it travels only within the local segment and is discarded at every router boundary. If the device is on a different subnet, connect a host to the same segment and set the address explicitly.

docs.title: Finding an Address When Discovery Is Disabled
docs.text:
The picoScan100 can disable SICK's proprietary UDP-broadcast discovery for cybersecurity reasons. When disabled, it does not reply to the standard search in SOPAS ET or SICK AppManager, but it still announces its address through standard network mechanisms such as Gratuitous ARP.

Connect the sensor to your computer or a local network switch, capture packets on the relevant Ethernet interface in Wireshark, and apply the display filter:

arp

Locate an entry whose MAC address begins with 00:06:77, the SICK device prefix, and read its IP address from the ARP packet details.

On Windows, run arp -a from an elevated Command Prompt and locate an address whose MAC begins with 00-06-77. On Linux, run arp -n and locate a MAC beginning with 00:06:77. The corresponding IP address belongs to the sensor. These commands work only when the sensor is in the current subnet; to locate a sensor outside the default subnet, configure the network adapter with a wider subnet mask such as 255.0.0.0.

docs.title: Request Telegram (24 Bytes)
docs.text:
Each field is at a fixed position:

Request Telegram (24 Bytes): bytes, field, value / source, and description.

Bytes Field Value / source Description 0 CMD 0x10 Command identifier for a scan (discovery) request 1 isBC 0x00 Unicast/broadcast origin flag, set 0x00 even when broadcasting 2-3 Length 0x00 0x08 Payload length, big-endian; always 8 for discovery 4-9 Host MAC FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF Sender MAC; all-ones for a broadcast request 10-13 Request ID random 4 bytes Fresh random per telegram; devices echo it so you can match replies 14 Scan flag 0x01 Marks a scan request; the device ignores the telegram if this isn't 0x01 15 Reserved 0x00 Must be zero 16-19 Interface IP host address Host interface IPv4, one byte per octet (big-endian) 20-23 Subnet mask host mask Host subnet mask, one byte per octet (big-endian)

docs.title: Sending the Broadcast
docs.text:
sock = UDP_socket()
sock.set_option(SO_BROADCAST, 1)
sock.set_option(SO_RCVTIMEO, 5)
sock.bind(interface_ip, port=0)

requestID = random_bytes(4)
telegram = build_telegram(interface_ip, subnet_mask, requestID)
sock.sendto(telegram, dest="255.255.255.255", port=30718)

while True:
    data, sender = sock.recvfrom(1024)
    if timeout:
        break
    device = parse_response(data)
    print(device)

sock.close()

Do not stop after the first reply: keep receiving until the 5 s timeout expires so you collect every device.

docs.title: Parsing the Replies
docs.text:
Each reply is a variable-length packet whose configuration fields are tagged: a 4-byte ASCII tag, a 2-byte internal header, then the field bytes. To extract a field, find its tag, skip 2 bytes, read the defined number of bytes:

index = buffer.find(tag)      # 4-byte ASCII tag
start = index + 4 + 2         # skip tag (4) + internal header (2)
value = buffer[start : start + field_length]

Parsing the Replies: tag, field, size, and encoding.

Tag Field Size Encoding EIPa Device IP address 4 IPv4 big-endian ENMa Subnet mask 4 IPv4 big-endian EDGa Default gateway 4 IPv4 big-endian EDhc DHCP flag 1 0x01 = DHCP, 0x00 = static EMAC MAC address 6 hex bytes, MSB-first

If a tag isn't found, that field isn't present in the response.

docs.title: Platform Notes
docs.text:
Set SO_BROADCAST before sending, or the send fails. On a multi-homed host, bind the socket to the IP of the adapter on the device subnet so the broadcast leaves the correct network interface card. On Windows, set the sensor network profile to Private; a Public profile blocks the inbound unicast replies. See Getting started.

SICK's discovery tools perform the same broadcast with a GUI. Use them for a quick look; use the raw telegram above when you need discovery built into your own application or a headless provisioning script.

docs.title: Error Codes
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

The device reports problems with a customer error ID. The web interface shows the ID together with a short description and a recommended action. The following list is the general SICK error code list. Not every code applies to every device.

Error Codes: error ID, description, and action.

Error ID Description and action 110 The device is defective. Return the device after consulting your SICK contact. 120 Switch off the device and restart it after 20 seconds. If the error occurs repeatedly, contact your SICK contact. 130 The firmware update failed. Install the firmware again after 2 minutes. If that does not work, install the last working firmware. 140 The system plug is defective. Replace the system plug. 205 The firmware update failed. The device uses the last active firmware. Restart the firmware update after 2 minutes. 210 The device is not ready for operation. Wait, and restart the device if the error persists. 211 Object evaluation is not active in interlaced mode. Deactivate interlaced mode to use object evaluation. 215 Measurement data is missing. 220 The device temperature is not OK. Check the ambient operating temperature. If necessary, use a heater or ensure sufficient cooling. 223 The device temperature is too low. Check the ambient operating temperature. If necessary, use a heater. 225 The device temperature is too high. Check the ambient operating temperature. If necessary, ensure sufficient cooling. 227 The motor speed is not OK. Check the device for external mechanical influences. 228 Shock or vibration exceeds the specification. 229 Dazzling detected. 230 The device is contaminated and not ready for operation. Clean the optics cover. 235 The device is not ready for operation. Wait. If the error persists, contact your SICK contact. 237 The device is not ready for operation. A parameterization problem was detected. Restart the device. If that does not help, contact your SICK contact. 239 Internal communication error detected. Switch off the device and restart it after 20 seconds. 240 The device and the system plug are not connected correctly. Check the connection and clean it if necessary. If the error occurs repeatedly, contact your SICK contact. 241 New system plug detected. The available inputs and outputs may have changed. Check the input and output configuration and all functions that use inputs and outputs. 250 The inertial measurement unit (IMU) is faulty. Restart the device. If that does not help, return the device after consulting your SICK contact. 505 Fallback mode is active. Disconnect the device from the power supply for about 20 seconds and restart it. 510 The device is temporarily not receiving measurement data. 511 The rotation speed deviates from the target value but is within the tolerated range: (f ≥ 15 Hz and f < 19 Hz) or (f > 21 Hz and f ≤ 25 Hz). Measurement data is still output. 512 The environment is too bright. The camera cannot capture the scene reliably. Adjust the lighting conditions. 513 The environment is too dark. The camera cannot capture the scene reliably. Increase the lighting. 520 The heater cannot be switched on. Check the power supply and the cable length and cross-section. 523 The temperature is close to the lower temperature limit. 525 The temperature is close to the upper temperature limit. 530 The device is contaminated and has limited functionality. Clean the optics cover. 540 Check the communication connection and settings. 541 Communication with the external CAN module is not possible. Check the wiring and the system parameterization. 543 A data packet could not be sent because a previous packet was not transmitted completely. Possible causes are a slow network connection or delayed data processing on the receiver side. Receive the data in a separate thread and use sufficiently large buffers. 545 Communication with the external time server (PTP, NTP) is not possible. Check the network settings. 547 The synchronization signal is missing. Check the wiring and the settings of the sync primary. 550 No connection to the internal additional sensors. Wait, and restart the device if necessary. 551 Measurement data of the inertial measurement unit (IMU) is missing. 560 I/O problem detected. Check the wiring and the configuration of the inputs and outputs. 562 The system plug memory could not be read. The system plug is defective or contains no data. Save the parameter set permanently on the system plug. If the error persists, check how the system plug is mounted on the device and replace the system plug if necessary. 563 The system plug memory could not be written. Check how the system plug is mounted on the device. 564 The input voltage is too high. Check whether the device is damaged. 565 The input voltage is too low. Inputs and outputs no longer work. 570 Parameterization problem detected. Check the configured parameters. 580 The HTTPS settings are faulty. Check the certificate on the Cybersecurity page. 581 Error while processing the certificate. Restart the device. If that does not help, return the device after consulting your SICK contact. 610 Too many fields are active at the same time. Reduce the number of simultaneously active fields or adjust the field size. 709 System plug without Gigabit Ethernet detected. This can cause loss of measurement data. Use a Gigabit Ethernet system plug. 710 Customer-specific setting. 715 The laser is switched off automatically by a customer-specific setting. 720 The device parameters differ from those on the cloning plug. The parameters from the cloning plug are applied. 810 Service mode. 905 The application is not loaded or not activated. Check the firmware. 907 The operation could not be completed because licenses are missing. Activate the required licenses and repeat the operation. 910 Too many functions are active at the same time. Deactivate functions that are not needed. 911 Object tracking is overloaded, for example because the device is moving. Switch off the object tracking function. 916 The output data is invalid. Restart the device. 917 Application error: Check your own programmed application or reinstall the SensorApp of the device. See the product documentation for details. 918 Application error: See Diagnostics in the user interface of the application or the product documentation. 920 No CAN data or invalid CAN data received. Restart the device. 921 The CAN interface configuration is invalid or causes conflicts on the CAN bus. Check the configured parameters on the Inputs and Outputs page. 935 One of the inputs used is not available or is used more than once. Check the functions that use ports as inputs. 940 The device is not ready for operation. Restart the device. If the error still occurs, reset the device to factory settings or change the parameterization. 990 Application error: The parameters are invalid. Check the configured parameters. If necessary, reset to factory settings. 992 The configuration was not applied because of an internal error. The device uses the last saved configuration. Configure the device again. If that does not work, restart the device.

docs.title: Firmware Update
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

The available update methods depend on the product family and firmware. multiScan100 firmware can be updated through SOPAS ET, Sentio Creator, the web UI (SOPASair), or supported REST endpoints. LRS4000 firmware can be updated through SOPAS ET or SICK AppManager. Check the product-specific release notes before updating.

docs.title: Where to Get the Package
docs.text:
Download the package that matches your device and target version from the device's product page on sick.com under Downloads / Software.

  • picoScan100
  • multiScan100
  • multiScan200
  • LRS4000

For multiScan100, multiScan200, and picoScan100, Sentio Creator, which can also provide firmware packages as well.

Read the release notes for your device before you update: LRS4000, multiScan100, multiScan200, or picoScan100.

docs.title: Web GUI
docs.text:
Open the device's firmware page in SOPASair and follow the update workflow.

Firmware update in the Web GUI.

docs.title: Sentio Creator
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Use Sentio Creator to discover the device, select the firmware version, and install the update.

Firmware update in Sentio Creator.

docs.title: Headless via the REST API
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Automate the update with the five steps below. Run them in order; skipping or reordering steps can leave the device in an inconsistent state. After flashing, the device reboots automatically and is unreachable for a few minutes. The update is successful only when the device is back online with the expected version.

docs.title: Get a Session Token
docs.text:
multiScan200 and picoScan100 use POST /api/CreateSessionToken at Service level with challenge-response in the JSON body. This endpoint also accepts HTTP Basic authentication, which is convenient in scripts:

POST /api/CreateSessionToken
Authorization: Basic <base64(Service:<password>)>
Content-Type: application/json

{}

Basic authentication sends the password only Base64-encoded. Use it only over HTTPS or on an isolated network.

The response contains the session token:

{ "header": { "status": 0 }, "data": { "token": "eyJhbGci..." } }

The multiScan100 REST interface documents /update, RunFirmwareUpdate, and UpdateState, but not CreateSessionToken. Use the authentication flow from the release notes or the OpenAPI file for the installed firmware.

docs.title: Upload the Package
docs.text:
PUT /api/update with the firmware file as the binary body. On multiScan200 and picoScan100, the X-Session-Token header authorizes this transfer, so Basic Auth is not required here.

PUT /api/update
X-Session-Token: <token>
Content-Type: application/octet-stream

<binary firmware file content>

A 200 OK confirms the package was received.

docs.title: Start the Update
docs.text:
RunFirmwareUpdate is a protected method requiring challenge-response in the JSON body. Basic Auth and the session token are not accepted here, so fetch a fresh challenge immediately before calling it.

POST /api/RunFirmwareUpdate
Content-Type: application/json

Fetch a fresh challenge and compute the hash for POST:RunFirmwareUpdate, then send it in the JSON body:

{
  "header": {
    "nonce": "...",
    "opaque": "...",
    "realm": "...",
    "user": "Service",
    "response": "<computed hash>"
  }
}

docs.title: Poll the Update State
docs.text:
GET /api/UpdateState every ~5 s until it reaches Finished (2) or the device becomes unreachable (reboot started). Stop on Error (3) and investigate before retrying.

GET /api/UpdateState

Example response:

{ "data": { "UpdateState": 1 } }

docs.title: Verify the New Version
docs.text:
After the device is back online, read the identity and compare against the expected version:

GET /api/DeviceIdent

Example response:

{ "data": { "DeviceIdent": { "Name": "picoScan", "Version": "2.3.3.0R" } } }

DeviceIdent.Version and GET /api/FirmwareVersion may format the same firmware version slightly differently, so normalize them before comparing.

docs.title: UpdateState Values
docs.text:
UpdateState Values: value, state, and meaning.

Value State Meaning 0 Initial No update in progress. Package may be uploaded but flashing hasn't started. 1 Started Flashing in progress. Do not power-cycle the device. 2 Finished Flash complete; the device reboots automatically. 3 Error Update failed. Check package compatibility and retry. Do not power-cycle immediately.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
• PUT /api/update returns 403: Missing or expired session token. Create a fresh token and add X-Session-Token.
  • RunFirmwareUpdate returns header.status 4 (Access Denied) or 10 (Invalid Challenge): Basic Auth or the session token was used instead of challenge-response, or the challenge was invalidated. Use a new challenge for POST:RunFirmwareUpdate.
  • UpdateState = 3 (Error): Wrong package or an unsigned package on firmware V2.2.0 or later. Download the correct .spk.signed and retry.
  • Device never returns: Normal reboot takes 2-5 minutes. Wait and keep UDP sockets open across the reboot.

While UpdateState is Started (1), never power-cycle the device. Allow 2-5 minutes total for the flash and reboot. Keep measurement sockets open across the reboot, so the OS doesn't buffer an ICMP port-unreachable message that would break the first recv() call afterwards (on Windows, apply SIO_UDP_CONNRESET).

On picoScan100, subscribe to the UpdateState WebSocket event instead of polling to get progress pushes during the flash. On multiScan200 and picoScan100, verify integrity after the update with the LFTchecksum: a firmware change updates MD5LinuxRoot and MD5App but leaves MD5Parameters and MD5Calibration untouched.

docs.title: Related Articles
docs.text:
How to perform a firmware update via HTTP.

How to perform a firmware update with SOPASair.

How to perform a firmware update with SOPAS ET.

docs.title: LiDAR License Management
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Some device functions require a license. Use the device's license manager to transfer an issued license code to the device. The exact screens and available options can vary by device and firmware.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
• Obtain a valid license code for the device. The code is formatted as five groups separated by hyphens.
  • Connect to the device and open its web interface.

docs.title: Activate a License
docs.text:
1. In a browser, connect to the device at http://<device-IP-address>/. On the device overview, choose View licenses.

Open the license overview from the device home page.

  1. In the license overview, choose Activate license.

The license overview also provides the action to deactivate returnable licenses.

  1. Select whether the device has an internet connection for the transfer, then choose Next.

Choose the transfer route that matches the device's network access.

  1. Enter or copy the license code. If the license ticket contains several entries, select the license entries to transfer, then continue.

Select the entries that should be transferred to the device.

  1. When the transfer succeeds, close the confirmation and check the updated license overview.

  2. Reboot the device.

docs.title: Deactivate or Return a License
docs.text: In the license overview, choose Deactivate license. During license selection, enter the license code for the license to deactivate, choose a license marked as returnable, then continue and confirm.

docs.title: Time Synchronization
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

This page describes how to synchronize sensor clocks with NTP or other time sources. Accurate timestamps help you align measurements from multiple sensors and correlate scans with external system events.

docs.title: NTP Time Synchronization
docs.text:
NTP synchronizes the sensor clock with an NTP server on the network. Use it when timestamps must match a common time base across systems, such as recorded sensor data, logs, or external applications.

An Ubuntu host on the sensor network can provide a shared clock without Internet access. Install and start the NTP service to set up an offline Ubuntu NTP server:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install ntp
sudo systemctl enable --now ntp

Configure /etc/ntp.conf to use the host's local clock and accept local queries:

server 127.127.1.0 prefer
fudge 127.127.1.0 stratum 10
restrict 127.0.0.1
restrict ::1

Restart the service after changing the configuration:

sudo systemctl restart ntp

To configure the sensor as an NTP client in SOPASair, open Configuration → Basic settings → Date and system time, choose the time zone and update rate, and enter the Ubuntu host's IP address. Save the settings and allow time for the next configured update. The sensor status page shows when synchronization completes.

Date and system time tile in SOPASair.

Through the REST API, set TSCRole to 1 for NTP client mode and set TSCTCSrvAddr to the server address. TSCRole accepts 0 (no time synchronization), 1 (NTP client), and 3 (PTP slave); other values are rejected with header.status 9 (Illegal Value). The sensor cannot act as an NTP server. LSPdatetime reads the current sensor time and LSPsetdatetime sets it manually.

To verify connectivity, check the service and local time on Ubuntu with sudo systemctl status ntp and timedatectl. Test the server with ntpdate -q 127.0.0.1, inspect NTP packets with sudo tcpdump -i any udp port 123 -v, and permit NTP through UFW with sudo ufw allow 123/udp when UFW is enabled.

Ensure that the sensor can reach the selected NTP server through the configured network and firewall. See REST API / OpenAPI for parameter access.

docs.title: PTP Time Synchronization
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

PTP synchronizes the sensor clock with other devices on a local network using the Precision Time Protocol. Use it for high-precision timestamp alignment when data from multiple sensors or other time-sensitive systems must be fused.

Date and system time settings with PTP selected.

docs.title: Sensor Settings
docs.text: The sensor uses fixed IEEE 1588 PTPv2 End-to-End (E2E) settings. It operates as an ordinary clock receiving synchronization from a master. Step mode is detected automatically: software PTP uses one-step operation and hardware PTP uses two-step operation. Its clockClass is 255, indicating slave-only operation.

docs.title: Master Configuration
docs.text:
Configure the PTP grandmaster with settings compatible with the sensor:

Master Configuration: parameter and required value.

Parameter Required value PTP profile IEEE 1588 PTPv2 E2E Transport protocol UDPv4 logAnnounceInterval 1 (2 seconds) logSyncInterval 0 (1 second) announceReceiptTimeout 3 logMinDelayReqInterval 0 (1 second) Domain number 0

Enable PTP in the sensor time-synchronization settings, or set TSCRole to 3 through the REST API, then connect it to this compatible PTP grandmaster. All participating devices must use the same domain, and network infrastructure must forward PTP traffic correctly.

With native ROS 2 on multiScan200 and picoScan100, the device publishes its hardware PTP timestamp in each message header. See Native ROS 2 for the available topics.

docs.title: User Levels
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

User levels control who can change the sensor configuration. Reading live data and status does not require a login, but configuration changes, methods, and protected API requests do.

User Levels: user level and factory state on multiScan200 and picoScan100.

User level Factory state on multiScan200 and picoScan100 Service Enabled Maintenance Disabled Authorized Client Disabled

For multiScan200 and picoScan100, only Service is enabled in the documented factory state. Check the product documentation for the multiScan100 or LRS4000 variant to confirm its factory state. On devices where the other levels are disabled, a Service-level user must enable them before they can be selected. Activate only the levels required by the deployment, then assign and protect their passwords before handing the system over.

docs.title: Enabling a User Level
docs.text:
Log in to SOPASair with the Service user level, open the user-level management settings, enable the required level, and set its password. Save the configuration permanently with Write EEPROM so the setting persists after a power cycle.

Access this tile in SOPASair via Diagnostic → Cybersecurity.

REST API clients enable or disable REST user levels with EnableUserLevel. In the challenge-response header.user field, write the levels as Service, Maintenance, and AuthorizedClient. CoLa A/B clients use EnableLegacyUserLevel for their respective user levels. Authenticate these changes as Service, and use a fresh challenge-response value for each protected REST request.

See REST API / OpenAPI for REST authentication and Challenge Response Authentication for the request flow.

docs.title: Resetting the Password
docs.text:
1. Establish a connection to the product in the web browser.
  2. Select Log In.
  3. Select Password forgotten?.
  4. Send the device key, serial number, and part number by email to the responsible SICK sales company or the responsible SICK service partner, see sick.com/worldwide.
  5. Click Next to confirm.
  6. The window for entering a code appears. You can get the code from the responsible SICK sales company or the responsible SICK service partner. The code is only valid once for the reset process. You can close the window by clicking on the x without interrupting the reset process. If you select Cancel or enter an incorrect code several times, the current reset process is terminated. The requested code is no longer valid. The process must be restarted.
  7. Optional: close the window. At a later time, open the window for entering the code via Settings and Password forgotten?.
  8. Enter the code.
  9. Click Reset to confirm.
  10. The password is reset to the default password. Parameters are not changed.

docs.title: NVIDIA Isaac Sim
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 picoScan100

NVIDIA Isaac Sim provides simulation environments for robotics, industrial automation, and autonomous systems. SICK LiDAR models let you test applications and algorithms before physical hardware is available.

SICK models are available for picoScan150, picoScan120, multiScan136, multiScan165, LRS4581R, and MRS1000. Find them on the applicable SICK product page under Downloads > Software or in NVIDIA Omniverse's sensor library. Configure the mounting position, orientation, field of view, scan frequency, detection range, and environment to match the deployment.

Product download areas:

  • LRS4000
  • multiScan100
  • picoScan100

Simulated SICK LiDAR scanning railway tracks in NVIDIA Omniverse, with the point cloud overlaid on the scene.

For more details on Isaac Sim, see:

  • What is Isaac Sim
  • Getting Started Tutorials

docs.title: Virtual Sensor Lab
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

The SICK Virtual Sensor Lab is a cloud service that gives you a live, virtual SICK sensor in the browser. No hardware is required. It is the fastest way to explore a device's web UI before the physical sensor is on your desk.

Open it at devices.cloud.sick.com.

SICK Virtual Sensor Lab product selection interface.

docs.title: Choose a Visualization Tool
docs.text:
Choose a tool based on whether you need to configure a live sensor, manage devices and firmware, locate a device, or inspect point-cloud files.

Choose a Visualization Tool: tool, what it is for, advantages, trade-offs, and best fit.

Tool What it is for Advantages Trade-offs Best fit CloudCompare View and process saved 3D point clouds. Free and open source; useful for inspecting point-cloud files such as PCD without writing a viewer. Works on saved point-cloud files rather than configuring the live sensor; requires compatible exported data. Offline 3D point-cloud inspection and processing. ROS 2 rviz Visualize live ROS 2 topics and point clouds. Standard ROS 2 desktop viewer; easy to validate frame alignment and scan coverage. Requires ROS 2 to be running; it is a visualization tool, not a device configuration UI. Debugging ROS 2 data flow and verifying topic quality. Sentio Creator SICK software for device commissioning and firmware package access. Helps manage and commission SICK devices and provides a source for matching firmware packages. Requires installing and using a separate SICK software tool; it is focused on commissioning, not on point-cloud analysis. Device discovery/commissioning workflows and finding firmware packages. SOPAS ET Legacy SICK engineering tool. Can discover sensors on a local network when the IP address is unknown; related workflows include configuration import/export and CSV recording. Legacy and no longer maintained for picoScan100 commissioning or configuration; continue in SOPASair for supported setup. Finding a device on the local network or accessing a legacy workflow. SOPASair Configure and commission a sensor through its built-in web interface. Nothing to install; opens in a browser; supports live settings and interactive workflows such as field teach-in and firmware update. Requires a network connection to the sensor; intended for device setup and live operation, not offline 3D point-cloud analysis. Day-to-day setup, configuration, and commissioning.

These tools serve different stages: use SOPASair or Sentio Creator for the device, ROS 2 rviz for topic validation, SOPAS ET for legacy discovery tasks, and CloudCompare for offline point-cloud work.

docs.title: CloudCompare
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 picoScan100

CloudCompare is a free, open-source 3D point-cloud viewer and processing tool. You can use it to visualize .pcd files produced by 3D scan recording or by the sick_perception_sdk, without writing any viewer code yourself.

LiDAR point cloud displayed in CloudCompare 2.13.2.

docs.title: ROS 2 rviz
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Use rviz2 to inspect SICK LiDAR point clouds, laser scans, and coordinate frames from native ROS 2 or sick_scan_xd.

  1. Configure the sensor for ROS 2 output as described in ROS Integration.
  2. Start the ROS 2 middleware and sensor publisher. For native ROS 2, use Cyclone DDS; for sick_scan_xd, start the driver on the host.
  3. Confirm that ROS 2 can see the sensor topics:
ros2 topic list

For native ROS 2, /cloud/all_points is the combined point cloud. A sick_scan_xd launch can use different topic names; select the sensor_msgs/msg/PointCloud2 or sensor_msgs/msg/LaserScan topic shown by ros2 topic list. 4. Launch rviz2 in the same sourced ROS 2 environment:

rviz2
  1. In the left panel, add a display such as:
  2. PointCloud2 for a dense 3D point cloud,
  3. LaserScan for 2D planar output,
  4. TF to verify coordinate frames,
  5. Axes to confirm sensor orientation.
  6. Select the published topic, set the fixed frame, and check the sensor data against the expected field of view.

docs.title: If the Display Is Empty
docs.text:
Set Reliability Policy to match the publisher when rviz2 reports an incompatible QoS profile. Check that data arrives on the topic:

ros2 topic info --verbose /cloud/all_points
ros2 topic echo --once /cloud/all_points

Replace the topic for a sick_scan_xd launch. If data arrives but rviz2 shows a No transform error, set Fixed Frame to the message's header.frame_id, or publish the required static transform.

docs.title: Sentio Creator
docs.text:
Compatible with: multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

Sentio Creator is a SICK software tool, published on sick.com, used to configure and commission supported SICK devices. Alongside the device's product page, it is also a source for firmware update packages. Use it to obtain the correct package for your device variant before running a firmware update.

Sentio Creator software interface displaying device list and extensions manager.

docs.title: SOPAS ET
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

SOPAS ET is a legacy SICK engineering tool and is no longer maintained for picoScan100 commissioning or configuration. Use SOPASair for supported device setup and configuration workflows.

SOPAS Engineering Tool interface with device search and project view.

SOPAS ET can still be useful for discovering sensors on the local network. Use its network search to locate a device when its IP address is unknown, then continue commissioning in SOPASair or through the REST API.

Related articles in the SICK knowledge base:

How to search for the device with SOPAS ET.

docs.title: SOPASair
docs.text:
Compatible with: LRS4000 multiScan100 multiScan200 picoScan100

SOPASair is the sensor's built-in web UI, served directly from the device at http://192.168.0.1/ with factory settings. There is nothing to install: point a browser at the sensor. Use it to:

  • configure the settings available on the selected device,
  • draw or teach in field-evaluation zones where the device supports those functions,
  • update firmware through the web UI where supported, or use the documented REST sequence,
  • create a diagnostic file if the device provides that option.

Screen-by-screen walkthroughs are available for the LRS4000, multiScan100, and picoScan100. Available menus and functions vary by product family, variant, and firmware. For standard IP address settings, see Getting Started.

For measurement recordings, see the SOPASair Data recorder if that function is available on your device.

Live capture from a picoScan100's SOPASair web interface.
